speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: TRIBUTES TO CONTRIBUTION OF ORGANIZED AND GENERAL LABOUR
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure I speak for all hon. members in paying tribute to labour, whose day this is. We honour the contributions made by labour during the years since unions were first recognized in the early 1870's, when, as a result of the bill introduced by the government of Sir John A. Macdonald, recognition was given to the right of labour to organize.

subtopic: TRIBUTES TO CONTRIBUTION OF ORGANIZED AND GENERAL LABOUR
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: TRIBUTES TO CONTRIBUTION OF ORGANIZED AND GENERAL LABOUR
speechtext:
Then in 1894, during the regime of Sir John Thompson, legislation was passed both in this country and in the United States making the first Monday of September a day on which tribute would be paid to those who labour and to the importance of labour in the lives of all of us.
It is well that there should be this day when we give national recognition to the fact that every advance in our development is made possible by work. Labour has done much ffnd will do much now and in the future for the achievement of Canada's undeniable destiny. My hope is that on this day, as we review the contribution made by organized labour and by labour in general, all Canadians will join in paying tribute to those belonging to the ranks of labour.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: TRIBUTES TO CONTRIBUTION OF ORGANIZED AND GENERAL LABOUR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to comment on what the Prime Minister has said, may I say that perhaps one of the best ways in which we can give recognition to labour is to ourselves labour, as we are doing, on Labour day. May I also join with the Prime Minister in saying that increasing recognition of the rights and importance of labour has been given over the years by Canadian governments representing both our parties.
May I also put a statement of mine on the record for Labour day, Mr. Speaker, because it expresses, in perhaps better words than I could find on the spur of the moment, my views on this matter. This statement was issued by myself on behalf of our party on Saturday last, and is as follows:
It is with great pleasure that I join other Canadians in paying sincere tribute to the working
men and women who have contributed so magnificently to the growth and prosperity of our country.
Labour day is a good occasion to recall that the rights of labour, at times hard won through stern struggle, are now regarded by all good citizens as an indispensable element of a free society.
These* rights must be maintained and even extended just as the responsibilities that go with them are accepted and discharged.
I am certain that labour will continue to make an invaluable contribution to the development of Canada, and to ensure that all citizens participate to the fullest extent in the benefits that will flow from that development.

subtopic: TRIBUTES TO CONTRIBUTION OF ORGANIZED AND GENERAL LABOUR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the C.C.F., I wish to associate myself with the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition in paying on this Labour day a very well deserved tribute to Canadian labour. The whole fabric of our Canadian society, a free society, depends in large measure on the welfare, the freedom and the responsibility of labouring people in this country.
We have been fortunate in Canada in the past to have had a responsible trade union movement representing, as it does, more than 1,250,000 trade unionists, and we pay tribute at this time not only to organized labour but to all those Canadians who earn their living by toil.
As the Leader of the Opposition has said, we recognize Labour days in perhaps the best way in this house by conducting the public affairs of this nation. I think the greatest tribute we could pay to organized labour, to unorganized labour and to all Canadians who have labour in mind at this time would be so to order our affairs as to guarantee full employment and a high standard of living to all the working people of this country.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Monteith (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: STATEMENT ON PROSECUTION OF DOCTOR ON MANITOULIN ISLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Saturday, while I was unavoidably absent from the house, the Leader of the Oppositipn and the hon. member for Kootenay West asked questions relating to a charge laid against Dr. Michael Ash, a physician employed by my department to care for the Indians of Manitoulin island and attend the small cottage hospital operated by Indian health services at Manitowaning.
Dr. Ash is an eminently qualified English physician, who served with the R.A.M.C. in Africa and Burma and practised for ten years as a general consultant on London's Harley street. He became interested in coming to Canada and made inquiries at our medical immigration office in London. As the director of Indian health services was passing through that city on his way to the world health organization meeting in Geneva, Dr. Ash was interviewed and careful inquiries were made as to his ability as a physician. He was highly recommended by senior officers of the British ministry of health and others. Dr. Ash took up his present position as medical officer, grade 2, in March of this year.
Naturally it is the policy of this department, wherever possible, to employ Canadian citizens licensed to practise in the province where their duties take them. Licensing of physicians is under the college of physicians and surgeons in each province. I might point out, however, that there is a serious shortage of doctors who are prepared to take up duty in some of the more remote areas where the services of medical officers are required for the care of Indians and Eskimos.
In view of this shortage it has been necessary on occasion to employ physicians from outside Canada. Reciprocation exists between the United Kingdom and six or seven of the provinces, but unfortunately this reciprocation for registering and licensing does not exist between the province of Ontario and the United Kingdom. To obtain a licence to practise in Ontario, Dr. Ash would have to write a set of examinations set by the dominion medical council in order to obtain the degree of licentiate of the medical college of Canada.
It has been ruled by the Department of Justice that physicians fully employed by the federal government do not, of necessity, have to be licensed in any particular province unless they "profess to practise for gain". In other words, as long as they confine their

work to the position they occupy with this department, they cannot be legally required to obtain a licence, but if they were to practise medicine with the public it would be an infringement of the medical act of the province concerned.
This situation was explained to Dr. Ash, and he was instructed to treat non-Indians only when emergency cases came to his attention. This understanding was known to the other doctors of Manitoulin island and had their full approval.
The Ontario college of physicians and surgeons saw fit to send an investigator to Manitowaning who posed as an emergency case requiring treatment and medicine for the relief of severe pain. Dr. Ash treated him and gave him some tablets known as 222's, containing aspirin and codeine. He charged his patient $5 and issued him an official receipt, so that this money is returned to the Receiver General of Canada.
I might add, Mr. Speaker, that officials of my department suggested to the president and the registrar of the Ontario college of physicians and surgeons that they withdraw the charge that was laid as a result of this incident, but they refused to do so. In consultation with the Department of Justice, legal counsel was appointed to defend Dr. Ash. The charge was dismissed by the magistrate in Little Current on August 27 of this year.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I thank the minister for the statement he has given, and express the hope that the experience to which Dr. Ash has been subjected will not discourage the doctor in the fine service he is giving in Manitoulin island.

of National Defence school at Rockcliffe for children whose parents desire that their children should be given their education in the French language.

MR. ARGUE    REFERENCE TO ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS ON AUGUST 13
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege arising out of questions and answers as reported in Hansard on August 13. On that day, as a second question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, I asked:
-whether the wheat board has yet been able to establish buying prices for grain this year and, if not, whether those prices will be established within
the next few days.
In answer to my question the Minister of Trade and Commerce replied as follows, as

Privilege-Buying Prices for Grain reported at page 3455 of Hansard. I had asked two questions, and the minister said:
In answer to the second part, I have been advised that the wheat board has established buying prices for the various grades of wheat it sells, and an announcement to this effect will be made very shortly.
Then I asked a supplementary question as follows:
I wonder if the minister is able to say now whether those buying prices will be the same as last year or whether there would be some differences.
The minister replied:
When the announcement is made and the prices are published a comparison can be made with the prices for last year, but I have not got the figures in my head now.
I hold in my hand the Canada Gazette, part II, dated Wednesday, August 27, 1958, and on page 953 there is a copy of an order in council dealing with the establishment of buying prices for wheat, oats and barley. After the proper preamble it reads as follows:
Therefore, his excellency the governor general in council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, pursuant to the Canadian Wheat Board Act, is pleased hereby to approve the sums certain to be paid to producers selling and delivering to the board wheat, oats or barley of the grades set out in the schedule hereto during the period commencing on the 1st day of August, 1958, and ending on the 31st day of July, 1959.
My question of privilege is that the minister did not inform the house that he had recommended these buying prices two days before I asked my question; and since they were established on the recommendation of the minister I believe he would have knowledge of the action that took place. The second question had to do with the exact buying prices, to which the minister replied that he did not have the figures in mind at that time. I had asked whether the figures were the same as the previous year. There are a great many grades and if there had been changes I would not and did not expect the minister to know, but on checking the figures set forth in the order in council and the prices for the grades in the previous year I can find no change in the grades set forth. I find that they are exactly the same.
I feel that the answer was misleading, though I do not suggest deliberately so. The minister had the information, he recommended the order in council two days before, and the information was not given to the house.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: MR. ARGUE    REFERENCE TO ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS ON AUGUST 13
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there was no intention whatever to mislead the hon. member or any member of the House of Commons. The order in council had been passed and was transmitted to the wheat board. It was left to them to make the announcement in due course.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (for the Minister of Agriculture) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext:
That it is expedient that the houses of parliament approve the agreement between the government of Canada and the government of Saskatchewan respecting the South Saskatchewan river project, signed cn the 25th day of July, 1958, and that this house do approve the same.
He said: Mr. Speaker, there are things which one looks forward to achieving throughout the years. This is one of those days in that, on behalf of the Minister of Agriculture, I am able to move the motion in question to confirm the agreement for the building of the South Saskatchewan dam and irrigation project. Throughout the years I have been of those who have advocated the building of the dam in order to meet a situation which has existed in central and southern Saskatchewan for generations. Indeed, as one reads the history of the early development of the country and of our early explorers one is struck by the fact that from 1691 to the present time those areas in southern and central Saskatchewan, and also in the neighbouring provinces to a much lesser extent, have been subject to drought.
On July 25 the Minister of Agriculture announced that an agreement had been signed with the government of Saskatchewan providing for the construction of this project. As the house knows, this project has been under study for many years, and I am very

happy to be able to bring this agreement before the house, for it represents another of the promises made by this party in the days of opposition, as well as since forming a government, which is now being carried into effect.
While there have been conflicting opinions as to the usefulness of the project, the weight of official and public opinion is such as to justify the conclusion that the project will be of lasting benefit not only to the province of Saskatchewan and the people it will serve there, but that it will be a project which will constitute another major step in the national development plan of this government. The immediate benefits upon the completion of this project will be that an irrigation potential of 500,000 acres will be created; a power potential of 200,000 horsepower will be made available; ample water supplies for urban and industrial developments in southern Saskatchewan will be assured, and the water levels of the Saskatchewan and Qu'Appelle valleys will be placed in a position where use will be made of those waters which for tens of thousands of years have simply been wasted by working their way ultimately, without benefit to the surrounding area, into Hudson bay. In addition there will be the recreation and tourist values consequent upon this development. These benefits, of course, will not be realized immediately, but my hope is that within a generation this project will be an achievement of such importance that it will be recognized as an asset of national consequence.
The essential features of the agreement are that the dominion government will design and build the dam and the essential works required for creating the reservoir that will impound 8 million acre feet of water. The estimated cost of this reservoir is $96 million, of which the dominion government will pay 75 per cent and the provincial government 25 per cent. Whatever the additional cost may be, the provincial share will in no case exceed $25 million. Furthermore, the national government will pay 25 per cent of the cost of the penstocks required to produce that minimum of power to which I have referred already.
Furthermore, as to the province's share of the expenditure for the reservoir which, as I said, is 25 per cent of the amount and in any event, regardless of the cost of the reservoir, will not exceed $25 million, the national government will aid in financing one-half by an obligation under which the province has 20 years in which to repay at an interest rate representative of the current cost to Canada of long term borrowing, and a carrying charge of one-eighth of one per 57071-3-278J
South Saskatchewan River Project cent. In other words, Saskatchewan's share of the cost is to be paid annually as the work progresses, one-half of such share to be paid in cash and the remainder in 20 years under the loan plan to which I have made reference. Saskatchewan will construct, operate and maintain at its own expense all power and irrigation facilities. The province will relocate provincial highways and ferries affected by the dam and reservoir, and the national government will pay 75 per cent of the cost of this work up to the equivalent of standards existing at the date the agreement was entered into.
When the reservoir has been filled to a level that provides a minimum operating head, it and all related works will be transferred to the province of Saskatchewan and that province will be responsible for operation, water allocation, and other decisions arising from the use of the impounded waters. For a period of six years from the transfer of the reservoir to Saskatchewan the national government will furnish all work and materials for maintenance and assume the full cost. For the next four year period the Saskatchewan government will share such costs equally and will thereafter relieve the national government of all obligation for further construction and maintenance.
I believe, sir, that in presenting this motion I can say that it represents a step in the achievement of a national policy which is based on the belief that the national welfare demands positive action to meet maladjustment in particular regions and industries. I am hopeful that this motion will receive the general support of members in all parts of the house, and that in the years ahead we will be able to look back on this day, particularly in the province of Saskatchewan but in the western provinces as well and throughout the country, as having brought about the beginning of an achievement which will give hope to those in that area for the future and will lay still stronger the foundations of a national development program to assure a reasonable degree of equality of opportunity in all the provinces of this country.

subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext:
From July 25, Mr. Speaker, the day on which the Prime Minister made an announcement in respect to the South Saskatchewan river project, to date we have been led from one surprise to another. First of all it was an agreeable surprise when on July 25 the Prime Minister announced that the government had signed an agreement with Saskatchewan. Then it was a surprise also when on August 18 there appeared in Votes and Proceedings the motion which we are debating this morning. It is another surprise to see that the

South Saskatchewan River Project pay. In addition, the province will have to pay the cost of the power house, including 75 per cent of the cost of the penstocks, the federal government having agreed to pay 25 per cent of the cost of these installations. These, the province says, will cost $35 million.
There must also be taken into account the irrigation scheme. The building of canals and the pumping stations will cost, according to figures we read in the newspapers, another $45 million, and I think that estimate is conservative in view of the fact that so many pumping stations will have to be built. The share of the provincial government may eventually amount to more than $110 million, but if we take that figure it is surprising to see that it coincides with the figure mentioned in the report. In the report, of course, the cost of construction of the dam alone is estimated at $139 million, by which I mean the cost of the construction of both dams and of the facilities connected with them.
Thus we can presume that the cost of building those two dams and creating the reservoir will amount to much more than $100 million. We do not object to this, but we feel that the Prime Minister should have come forward and told us, "We are asking, now, for a revised estimate", or "We have asked the engineers to prepare new estimates".
However, this is not an objection. We do not object to that. What we object to is the fact that this motion has been presented in the form of a resolution simply to approve an agreement which has been entered into by both parties. The cost to the province will be quite high. I know that negotiations have gone on for 12 months because the province of Saskatchewan felt it should have had the same advantages that were extended to the maritimes with regard to the production of hydro-electric power. They certainly have something there. However, this government feels that all it can do in this respect is to pay 25 per cent of the cost of intall-ing penstocks in the dam and down to the power house.
There are many questions we should like to ask the Prime Minister, but I understand that Your Honour being in the chair we are not permitted to ask questions and have them answered back and forth. We can only ask the minister to give us some additional information, when he rises to reply and closes the debate, with regard to the timetable. When does the government intend to begin this work? I know the Prime Minister has said that as soon as an agreement could be signed the work would be started. When the Prime Minister said that,


he was anxious to see the work begun. However, we would like to be given this information with somewhat greater precision.
We should also like to ask the Prime Minister if it is the intention of the government to organize an authority to build the dam. I know that under the agreement there is mention of a board, and the duties of that board are outlined in part 6 of the agreement, on page 15:
21. (1) Canada and1 Saskatchewan will constitute a board of officials, to be called the South Saskatchewan river development board, to consist of seven members, four of whom, including the chairman, shall be appointed by Canada and three of whom shall be appointed by Saskatchewan, and the duties of the board shall be as follows:
(a)	to review the general design of the project with particular reference to the schedule of construction and the design relationships of the main dam and reservoir to ensure the most economic use of water for irrigation and electric power;
(b)	to maintain continuous liaison with the parties hereto and their agencies;
(c)	to correlate the planning and information required for the proper timing of construction;
(d)	to be fully informed of all construction work undertaken pursuant to this agreement; and
(e)	to advise upon accounting and records procedures required for the sharing of costs and the payment thereof.
But, Mr. Speaker, we are not sure if this board will decide on contracts, for instance. We do not know if the board will see that tenders are called. I can understand that this board would be a body acting between the government of Canada and the government of the province of Saskatchewan in respect to those matters which are outlined on page 16.
Another question to which we would like an answer is this. Has the government established a timetable for the work? We have read in various reports that the work will take a considerable length of time to complete. First there was mention of a period of eight or ten years, but now we are told in the report of the royal commission and by the P.F.R.A. that the work can be done in six years. So much the better. At the end of six years there will be a period during which the federal government will operate and maintain the reservoir, and then the reservoir will be transferred to the province following that period. These are matters on which we would like to have clear answers.
Another question of interest to us is this. Has the government prepared a final estimate? I mentioned that we were worried because we have had only a rough figure of $96 million. In view of the fact that some figures of the royal commission report for the construction of the dam have been used, we feel they will probably be closer to reality.
There are many other things we would like to know. For instance, is it the intention

of the government to have this agreement approved by both houses of parliament and then perhaps next year present a bill to proceed with the work? Of course this would be quite good publicity for the government. One year we have a resolution and the next year we have a bill. I observe that the Prime Minister is shaking his head; apparently he is saying no. We would have hoped the government would have come forward with a bill in which would have been incorporated all the things I mentioned at the beginning of my remarks including the cost, the amount of money the federal government intends to spend to realize this project, and many other things.
There is another important question mentioned in the report of the royal commission of 1952. According to contractors, men who have had some experience in the building of large projects, it would be of advantage for the government to give one main contract. It may be that the government intends to give one main contract for the construction of both dams in order to fill the reservoir. On the other hand, perhaps the government intends to give separate contracts for each dam. Perhaps it intends to give separate contracts for building the construction sites and for building the necessary roads to proceed with the job. Those are the things we would like to know about, and when the Prime Minister closes the debate I trust he will answer these questions.
I do not wish to take too much of the time of the house. As I have already said, we were disappointed that a bill was not introduced. It is true that certain amounts of money are included in the estimates. There is a small amount in the main estimates and a substantial amount in the supplementary estimates; but those estimates came before the house on August 1, the day the agreement was tabled. I would not swear to it, but I believe it was not mentioned that the agreement had been tabled or, if it was mentioned, I would point out that it was tabled the same day the Minister of Agriculture completed his estimates. Therefore I will ask the Prime Minister to answer some of the questions I have raised.
May I repeat that we would have preferred to have a bill. While we are anxious to see this project proceeded with, and while we do not disapprove of the agreement contained in the document consisting of 17 pages, we do disapprove of the procedure adopted by the government in this regard. For this reason I move, seconded by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan):
That all the words after "1958" in the resolution be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"but that this approval be not given until a measure preceded by the recommendation of the
South Saskatchewan River Project Governor General thereto has been introduced by the government providing for the authorization of the necessary expenditures for the whole project."

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext:
While this amendment might be appropriate on a bill, I am not clear that it is in order on a resolution. I should like to refer the hon. member who has moved the amendment to the obstacles which I see to it, in case he has some citation or authority which would change the view which appears to me to be appropriate at this time. Citation 203 of Beauchesne's "Parliamentary Rules and Forms", fourth edition, deals with amendments. Paragraph (1) reads:
It is an imperative rule that every amendment must be relevant to the question on which the amendment is proposed. Every amendment proposed to be made either to a question or to a proposed amendment should be so framed that if agreed to by the house the question or amendment as amended would be intelligible and consistent with itself.
The law on the relevancy of amendments is that if they are on the same subject matter with the original motion, they are admissible, but not when foreign thereto.
This amendment does not propose to deal with the motion before the house at all; it proposes to declare that some other course of action should be taken which I think is really declaratory of a principle. That sort of amendment is dealt with by Beauchesne in his third edition, in citation 346 at page 137, where he says:
Moreover, the amendment could not be a declaration of principles because the only motions on which such a declaration can be moved are motions for the address in reply to the speech from the throne, motions to go into committee of supply or ways and means and for the second reading of public bills.
On that basis it seems to me that the relevancy of the amendment must be that it relates to the subject matter of the resolution. This proposed amendment does not seek to modify the resolution; it seeks to dispose of it altogether on the basis that the government should have taken some other course. Before I rule the proposed amendment out of order I would like to hear hon. gentlemen on it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is an historic day not only for Canada but more particularly for the people of Saskatchewan. It demonstrates very clearly that when the people of a province are united, as the people of Saskatchewan have been for so many years in asking for the building of this dam on the South Saskatchewan river, no matter what the obstacles, no matter how many learned commissions may inquire into the proposition, their united faith and determination will win through against all obstacles.
To a very considerable degree the debate on this motion and its adoption are nonpolitical matters. Over the years the Prime Minister has been consistent in his advocacy of a dam on the South Saskatchewan river. He has been consistent, and he has been a very persuasive advocate of this proposition.
I said it was a matter which commended the support of the people of Saskatchewan without regard to politics. I think that was true even under the former Liberal administration. For many years we had in this house Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner as minister of agriculture. I am sure no one doubts that Mr. Gardiner was fully in support of this proposition. When Jimmie spoke on the floor of the house one was not always able to ascertain that he personally was in favour of it, because he was a very excellent debater and apologist for the cabinet on any given proposition. Nonetheless his stand has been consistent, and I am sure that he, with all other residents of Saskatchewan, will rejoice that this step is being taken.
The premier of Saskatchewan, who signed the agreement on behalf of that province,

has been a firm champion of the South Saskatchewan river project both as a member of parliament from 1935 to 1944 and subsequently as premier of the province and I think, together with the Prime Minister, his faith is amply demonstrated by the agreement that has been signed.
The hon. member for Villeneuve made a very interesting speech. While he comes from another province, he has shown that by applying himself to the subject he has been able to obtain an excellent grasp of its many details. I think it is rather important to note that the spokesman for the official opposition in this debate represents a constituency in the province of Quebec. This is further proof to me of something I have believed for a long time; that although the main benefits of a given project before parliament will accrue to a particular section of the country, members from all areas will forget their regional differences and support such a project as in the national interest even though its primary benefits will be felt by the people of another province.
I do not want to open old wounds, but I am further convinced in my attitude by the statement of the hon. member for Villeneuve that the former prime minister was not right when he said the project was not in the national interest, or that he had not been convinced that it was in the national interest. We see a member from the province of Quebec speaking for the official opposition who, while asking many questions and suggesting an alternative procedure, has left no doubt that the official opposition will support the project.
This year, 1958, is perhaps a good year to proceed with the dam, as it is a year of widespread drought in the province of Saskatchewan. The degree of drought was not nearly as bad as some of us feared some weeks ago; nevertheless Saskatchewan faces a short crop and in various areas there is a difficult feed problem. This summer the people of Saskatchewan and the South Saskatchewan river development association once again demonstrated their faith in the project at a meeting at Outlook which 700 persons attended for the purpose of lending their support to the proposition that a dam should be built on the South Saskatchewan river.
It has been said by the deputy minister of agriculture of Saskatchewan, and again this is something with which everyone will agree, that the project will stabilize feed reserves within a radius of 150 miles from the site of the dam. If this is true, and I believe it is, it will mean the stabilization of the fodder supply for farmers year in and year out, 57071-3-279
South Saskatchewan River Project no matter whether the crop is good or bad, over an area of 70,000 square miles or 45 million acres.
The dam will also provide certain power facilities and, as the Prime Minister has said, will result in the irrigation of a maximum of 500,000 acres. We in Saskatchewan expect that this will go a long way toward providing a substantial measure of industrialization in the years ahead.
While it may be impossible to prove from a cost accounting standpoint that all the money going into the development will be returned with interest, I believe time will show that it was a good, sound investment from the national point of view, and that together with the direct dividends the indirect dividends that will flow from the project will more than warrant the action parliament is taking today.
I think the project is being proceeded with at an auspicious time because of the slackness in the Canadian economy, although I do not want anyone to think we believe we should have waited until there was a degree of slackness in the economy before starting the dam. We are hoping that work will be started immediately, and that as construction is launched it will reduce unemployment in the nation very materially and provide for the taking up of part of the slack in our economy. It has been estimated that the project will take 18 million man hours and probably a work force of 1,800 men plus machinery to lay one million cubic yards of concrete and 50,000 tons of structural steel. These materials will go to build a dam 250 feet high and 8,000 feet long which will provide a main reservoir covering 8 million acres which will be 140 miles long, with a shore line of between 400 and 500 miles.
It has been estimated that the total cost of the project will be $180 million. I have said that this proposition is supported by all the people of Saskatchewan. I hope and expect that when the vote is taken on the resolution it will be passed unanimously. But I do not think that the public should assume that this is a hand-out or gift to the province of Saskatchewan, because it is a joint project toward which both Saskatchewan and the federal government will pay very large sums of money. Of the total estimated cost of $180 million it is estimated that the total federal government contribution will be $74 million. Therefore the people of Saskatchewan will be paying directly more than half the total cost of the project when completed.
It has been said that next year will mark the one hundredth anniversary of the time the project was first suggested. However, since 1935 it has been put forward as an idea

South Saskatchewan River Project that might be fulfilled within a short time and the Liberal government, through its minister of agriculture from Saskatchewan, did not hesitate on every occasion to set out the advantages that would flow from the project. We had always understood, in the early days of discussion, that the federal government was to bear responsibility for the project. As the years have gone on, more and more of the cost has been laid upon the province of Saskatchewan. In 1953 the present Prime Minister in speaking on this particular point had this to say, as recorded on page 1586 of Hansard for February 3, 1953:
Then on May 31, 1951, for the first time to my knowledge, a suggestion was made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) that it would be necessary for the province of Saskatchewan to accept the responsibility of providing irrigation facilities. Until that time I had never heard, nor am I able to find any record anywhere, that there was any responsibility to fall upon the province of Saskatchewan.
Those were the words of the present Prime Minister speaking in this house at that time. It was clearly stated by the Liberal government that Saskatchewan would have to bear the cost of providing irrigation facilities. We had expected, in the light of order in council P.C. 2298 of June 19, 1947, that in addition to the dam the main irrigation canals would be maintained by the federal government. In this instance I think I am correct when I say that these main irrigation canals will be a responsibility which must be borne by the provincial government. In the order in council to which I have just referred it was made very clear that when the federal government built the dam, that is the main dam and the main canals, the federal government would operate those projects. In paragraph 4 of this order in council there are these words:
In the construction of an Irrigation project hereunder, Canada will undertake and assume responsibility for the construction of the main reservoirs and any connecting canals and will be responsible for the maintenance and operation of such works;-
This was laid down as an over-all condition for all main irrigation programs in Canada by the former Liberal administration. It is true that this did not apply to Saskatchewan. It was not applied to Saskatchewan because we were not given the opportunity of proceeding with the dam. Nevertheless that was the overriding condition, and it was to apply when such an agreement was signed. We find now, after a period of ten years and in the face of great opposition from Saskatchewan, that the main dam is to be turned over to the province for operation. Saskatchewan would have preferred that the operation of this dam be


assumed by the federal government in perpetuity. This is another responsibility that the Saskatchewan government has been asked to assume.
Then Saskatchewan has been asked to pay not only for the installation of power facilities at the dam site, but also a portion of the cost of construction of the dam itself. The main dam, it is estimated, will cost $96 million and Saskatchewan has to pay 25 per cent of this amount or $24 million, with a ceiling of $25 million because a ceiling has been written into the agreement. This is another cost that Saskatchewan must pay. When the negotiations for this agreement were taking place Saskatchewan asked for a $20 million loan to provide power facilities. This loan was not granted, although agreement was given to a loan for half the 25 per cent of the cost of the dam for power purposes.
Then, of course, there was the whole question of damage to property of third persons if the dam should go out, either as the result of faulty construction or because of flash floods or some other act of God. The government has gone some distance in agreeing that it would assume this responsibility under certain conditions, but a substantial part of this responsibility may be left with the province.
These are some of the steps that have been taken as the negotiations have been conducted, and which have led to greater and greater burdens being accepted by Saskatchewan. If Saskatchewan had turned them down there would be no dam.
I do not believe this is the final agreement. I do not believe this agreement will stand forever in this final form, or will even stand in this form during the life of the members of this house. I feel that Saskatchewan has a case for asking, in the years ahead, for the federal government to assume a larger share of these costs. I have no doubt that Saskatchewan, no matter what the composition of the legislature, will unanimously request the federal government from time to time to be more generous in its sharing of the costs than is set forth in this agreement, just as the legislature gave unanimous approval to this agreement.
This will be a very heavy burden upon the treasury of Saskatchewan. It is estimated that the share of the Saskatchewan people, apart from their share of the federal proportion as citizens of this country, will total $110 million. This is a severe burden on any province and it will be a large burden on a province like Saskatchewan, even though Saskatchewan revenues continue, as they have in recent years, to expand and improve. In addition to

the heavy burden that comes from the provision of this sum of money itself, the burden will further be increased-and no one can deny this-by the financial policies that have been proceeded with by this government during this session. The reconversion loan will make moneys for provincial projects more expensive, and will add to the cost to be born by the Saskatchewan treasury.
In my remarks I have said this is a project that appeals to the citizens in Saskatchewan of all political parties. I give it my full and wholehearted approval. The people of Saskatchewan will rejoice as they see this project proceeded with in the years ahead. There may be instances when we feel, so far as the power loan is concerned or other aspects, that we have a greater claim on the federal treasury, especially in the light of what is being done in other parts of Canada, than the government is prepared to accept at a given time. However, we are good Canadians and we shall support similar projects in other regions when they have a similar value for the residents of those regions. We do hope and we are confident that in the days ahead the terms for the province of Saskatchewan will be improved and that this very important joint project will prove to be one of the best undertakings the Saskatchewan government and the federal government have ever undertaken.

speechtext:
As
the member for Rosetown-Biggar, where the South Saskatchewan dam will be located, I should like to tell hon. members about some of the ways in which we will benefit from this great project. First I would like to say that this is not a new project; it has been spoken of for years. In fact the first time the South Saskatchewan river dam was mentioned, according to a little story, was during the period of drought before Saskatchewan became a province and when it was part of the Northwest Territories. During this period of drought all the buffalo and antelope had left for greener pastures in the north, and the Indians on the plains were starving. One day, away on the horizon, a band of Indians saw a herd of buffalo and the chief called together his braves and picked from them his best hunters. He put them on the fastest horses and sent them out to bring in some meat to his starving tribe. After riding for many miles they came to the Saskatchewan river and there, on the other side, they saw the herd of buffalo peacefully grazing on the banks. One of the braves looked across the river and said, "Damn that river." That was the first mention of the South Saskatchewan river dam.
To be more serious, it was in the 1850's that a party of men headed by a Mr. Palliser was
57071-3-279J
South Saskatchewan River Project sent into the Northwest Territories to see what the value of that country would be west of the rockbound shores of lake Superior. The party spent about six years there and eventually brought back a report to the effect that it was a short grass, treeless country, the land being very fertile, but owing to the long period of drought it would never be fit for agriculture. Mention was made of this great river running across the plains which could be dammed up and the water used for irrigation purposes. Nothing was done, however, until the great drought of the thirties, when the people realized that something had to be done to improve conditions on the prairies and they began to study the feasibility of a South Saskatchewan river dam. After years of study, negotiation and no action, I now have the privilege of supporting a government which proposes to build that dam, so it will become an immediate reality.
I wish now to say a few words on the dam itself. The dam will be of earth construction, 205 feet high, 16,700 feet long and the water behind the dam will be 180 feet deep. This will create a lake 135 miles long with a shore line of 475 miles. One can realize from those figures just what the benefits will be. First, there will be recreational facilities including camping, boating, fishing and summer resorts within a two-hour drive of over half the population of Saskatchewan. The Qu'Ap-pelle valley starts on the Saskatchewan river at a point near Elbow, and the waters from the Saskatchewan river dam will flow down that valley to a depth of 80 feet. An auxiliary dam will be built in the Qu'Appelle valley to allow a gradual flow of water down the river, which will keep five beautiful lakes at their original levels. There are many summer homes and camping grounds built around these lakes, and in the 1930's the people looked out from their summer homes on to dry, dusty lake bottoms, so this is but a by-product of the main benefits which will be received when the South Saskatchewan river dam is built.
The next point with which I would like to deal is the domestic water supply. The thriving cities of Moose Jaw and Regina have spent millions of dollars on their water supply, and in late years they have tapped Buffalo lake in the Qu'Appelle valley. Yet they have only a two months' water supply during the dry period. In the 1930's there was a penalty imposed for using municipal water for washing your car or watering your garden and many of the beauty spots dried up, just as did the farmers' crops. Small towns and villages in Saskatchewan are presently passing bylaws for water works, sewage and sanitation, but the real problem

South Saskatchewan River Project is the water supply from the South Saskatchewan river. These reservoirs I have mentioned can be tapped so these small towns and villages can get an adequate water supply.
I shall be brief with respect to power. The dam will produce 210,000 horsepower or an average annual output of 475 million kilowatt hours. At the present time Saskatchewan power is generated through steam turbines. The hydro power to be produced by the South Saskatchewan river dam will give us an abundance of cheap power to aid in the development of the natural resources of the province.
I come now to the main purpose, that of irrigation. The present proposal is to irrigate 500,000 acres, which I feel will take 500,000 acres out of our one crop economy, wheat, and put agriculture in Saskatchewan on a more stable economic basis. 1 particularly have in mind the cattle industry. At one time we had a cattle industry, but during the drought period of the thirties our herds were cut down, the climax coming in 1937 when the government and the municipalities could only supply enough feed for one cow per farm for milking purposes. If you kept more than one cow you had to provide the feed. Then in 1937 the government bought up all the surplus stock at 1J cents and 2 cents per pound. After that experience the farmers were very reluctant to build up herds, but more recently the younger farmers have built up cattle herds of better quality and Saskatchewan now has more cattle than ever before. There is, however, always the danger of another drought period as a result of which the farmers would have to sacrifice their cattle as they did in the thirties.
Summer pasture is always a problem when it takes five acres of our native pasture to feed one cow. On the other hand, on irrigated pasture seven cows can be supported by one acre of land. This is typical of the benefits to be derived from the irrigation of 500,000 acres of the dry area of Saskatchewan.
Statistics show that the development of the area under P.F.A.A. meant the paying out of assistance totalling $10,200,000 during the period 1939 to 1950. Would it not have been better to have paid out this money for the construction of the dam? Further statistics show that the population in this area dropped from 32,000 in 1926 to 18,000 in 1951 because the small farms were being taken over by the larger ones, for only the larger ones could carry on under the dry conditions. We all know that we have to have population in order to prosper, and that we cannot attract people under existing conditions.


The hon. member for Medicine Hat stated in the house that we expect a land flowing with milk and honey, and that all our problems will be over when the South Saskatchewan river dam is finished. This is not correct, but we do expect a green oasis in Saskatchewan's dry belt, and we will benefit by the experience of our Alberta friends who have had the advantage of irrigation for some time. This is a long term project, but Saskatchewan farmers are quick to seize any opportunity to get away from a one crop economy dependent on wheat.
To sum up the benefits to be provided, they are the irrigation of 500,000 acres, cheap electric power development, improved domestic water supplies, recreation and tourist attractions.

I realize that perfectly well, and it is precisely the point I am coming to. That is precisely why, if I may refer to it, my hon. friend from Villeneuve made the motion he did, the motion which Your Honour ruled out of order and with regard to which we, of course, accept your judgment. I recognize that I am coming close to transgressing the rules when I say this, but we have heard in another place criticism by hon. members opposite of what is alleged to have been bits and pieces financing of a project which, compared with this one, is very small indeed; and it seems to me that if parliament is to make a real judgment on this matter it should consider the whole proposal as a legislative project in a fashion which would enable all hon. members to examine every aspect of the proposition.
I said, and of course we all know, that when this resolution is passed it will commit the government to absolutely nothing. All it does is commit the two houses to express the view that they approve this undertaking. But a resolution of the two houses, as again we all know, has no legal effect whatsoever; it is merely a pious expression of approval.
What we fear is that the government is going to use this expression of approval of the two houses as a blank cheque, as the hon. member for Villeneuve very correctly put it, and that they are going to bring in an estimate in respect of the amount of work which they feel can reasonably be done each year without this house at any time being given an opportunity to consider, with all the details before it, what should be the proper judgment of parliament with regard to a matter of this magnitude.
I am sure there is no one in the house- at least, I know of no hon. member of the house-who has any question in his mind but that this project in itself is a good thing; that it will be a very desirable thing to develop this hydro-electric power; that it will be a very desirable thing to have this great lake in south Saskatchewan; that it will be a very desirable thing to have this water available for irrigation. No one doubts that. But this country is filled with desirable projects which all of us, or some of us at any rate, would like to see developed.
South Saskatchewan River Project
It is, of course, the responsibility of parliament in appropriating money to make choices, because under our present system- and I hope it will long continue to be our system-the supply of money is not unlimited. It is our responsibility in appropriating money to make choices between desirable things and it is not possible, I submit, to make an intelligent choice on the basis of a resolution of this character.
What we should have before us, it seems to me, is a resolution with a message from the crown and a bill setting out the whole scheme, a bill which could be considered in committee and through all the stages that are provided with regard to money bills of that character. We will not be in committee on this resolution. Once a vote is taken on it the matter is disposed of as far as this house is concerned. We have no way of scrutinizing the agreement and no way of asking questions of the government with regard to the details of the agreement; no way of knowing, beyond what is in the text itself, how it is proposed to proceed to implement this agreement.
And when I said that it seemed to me this resolution was either a meaningless affair, a pious expression of good intention, or it was a new, improved and streamlined form of closure, I meant exactly what I said. I admit that the government and the Prime Minister are very clever at this kind of thing. I yield to no one in my admiration for the Prime Minister in this field, because he presents us with a dilemma. He says, "Either you vote against this resolution, in which case we will go all over the country saying you are against the South Saskatchewan dam, or you vote for it, and from then on every time you say a word in criticism we will get up and say you approved it".

Mr. Speaker, when we adjourned for the luncheon recess I had repeated a statement I made at the outset of my observations, and perhaps for the sake of continuity I should repeat it again, namely that this motion can be looked upon in one of two ways, either as a pious expression having no legal effect or as a new, improved, streamlined form of closure. I think all of us who were here recollect what happened in the parliament before last in the session of 1956.
To illustrate what I mean by the objectionable character, from the point of view of proper consideration by the house, of this project and the motion before us, I intend to indicate what conceivably could have happened in that session of parliament if a similar motion had been made. It will be recalled that what we were considering in the session of 1956 was a bill based on a resolution, a bill to implement an agreement made with the Trans-Canada Pipe Line Company and another agreement made with the government of Ontario. The only difference in principle between that situation and this is that there were two agreements instead of one. There was an agreement with this company and also an agreement with the provincial government.
If I apprehended correctly what the Prime Minister suggested when he interrupted me at one point, it seems to me it is the intention of the government once this motion has been accepted to proceed merely by annual estimates. This would have been on all fours with what might have been done in that case. In other words the government of that day in 1956 might have introduced a motion such as this to say it was expedient for the two houses to approve the agreement with the Trans-Canada Pipe Line Company and the agreement with the government of Ontario, and that this house do approve the same. That would have permitted debate on a motion that it is not too easy to amend, so that each hon. member except the mover could speak only once and there could be no opportunity to probe the agreements, to consider the details and to have the questions and answers at all the stages that are necessary in money bills concerning large projects of this character. Then all that would have been required would be the appropriate items in the estimates-I assume there would be
