All I want to do is say that it seems to me the procedure we are following denies to the opposition and indeed to private members who support the government who may want to probe into this matter a real opportunity to give it the kind of consideration it ought to have.

subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext: You have had ample occasion and opportunity.

subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext:
We have the agreement, but it is not a contract with anybody to do the work. It is merely an agreement with the province of Saskatchewan.
Mr. Pallet!: That is more than we got on the pipe line.

subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext:
It is merely an agreement with the province of Saskatchewan and nothing more. I admit that my argument would collapse in part at once if the Prime Minister were to get up at any stage and give us an assurance that before this project proceeded beyond the survey stage-which it is easy to understand should be done by items in the estimates, and quite properly-before the point had been reached at which it could not really be stopped, we would have a measure brought in with a message from the crown, as was done in the case of the pipe line and the St. Lawrence seaway and, as far as I can recollect, as has always been done with great national projects of this kind. Then what we would be doing today would be merely giving a kind of approval in principle to this agreement, and that would certainly be a great deal less objectionable; though it would still be objectionable, I submit, because no matter what attitude we may take in the matter it is going to create a false impression on the part of the public. It cannot help but do that.

We on this side of the house, having had the agreement only since August 25, cannot pretend to have scrutinized it with the care it should have had.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext: Was it not August 1?

subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext:
Surely it was long before
August 25. Was it not July 25?

subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext:
Well, in any event, with
the hours we have been sitting in this house and the kind of session we have had, whatever the date and without the capacity-

subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext:
That is right, without
the capacity.

subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext:
I was using the word
"capacity" in the sense in which it is used in the other official language of this country, that is to say without the opportunity of questioning the minister who would be responsible-

subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext:
But the government does
not want to provide an opportunity for questioning. This is a new form of closure.
Mr. Pallet!:	Nonsense.

subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext: What I am saying, Mr. Speaker, and the hon. member for Ottawa West said it better than I can, is that through the government following this procedure of bypassing the ordinary methods used in parliament, we will not have an opportunity to give this measure the kind of consideration parliament ought to give to so important a national project.

subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext: Why not let the hon. member for Ottawa West speak, then?

subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext: When we vote and however we vote on it, that vote is bound to be construed either as a vote against the project or as a vote in favour of the agreement.

subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext: Then don't vote.

subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext:
That is, of course, a
possibility that is open to us. That is a course that has been taken by certain hon. members in this house in times past, but it is one which I must say is rather repugnant to me.
Mr. Pallet!:	Oh, come, now; you walked
out of one the other night.

subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext:
It is a course which I
do not think is desirable. What I do say is that this is not the right way to embark upon a great national project of this sort. It does seem to me that since we shall have to make a choice in the circumstances in which we have been placed by the government-and I repeat that I have a great deal of admiration for the skill of the Prime
South Saskatchewan River Project Minister in devising these dilemmas-I do not know whether those slick procedures are precisely the kind of respect for the rights of parliament that the public were led to expect.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman a question. Will he tell the house what the government of which he was a member did in respect of the St. Mary's dam, on which up to the present time has been expended some $40 million? What was the course followed?

subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext:
With respect to the St.
Mary's dam, as I understand it, an item was put in the estimates-

subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext:
-and it was, of course, a project of a magnitude not in any way comparable with this one. Not only was it not comparable in any way with this one, but I suspect-and I am glad the Prime Minister has reminded me of it, because it does add great force to the argument I am making -that it is precisely because the government has very little confidence in its estimates of cost that it does not bring in a proper measure, with a proper estimate of the whole cost of this project. Everybody knows, of course, that the St. Mary's dam was started at a time when we were-I cannot remember the exact date; I cannot remember whether it was while we had price controls or just after they were lifted, but it was immediately after the war, at a time when the price level was very much lower than it is, unhappily, at the present time. Any estimates of cost at that time, of course, have been greatly exceeded in this project, and I suspect that exactly the same will be true in the case of the South Saskatchewan project.
That seems to me, sir, precisely the best argument for taking the proper course in this matter and giving the house a proper opportunity, under the rules for dealing with money bills, to envisage this whole project because, as I said at the beginning and I repeat, this project is going to cost a great deal of money. Because of its size it is not the kind of project that ought to be carried out merely by annual items in the estimates. Members of parliament should have the opportunity to exercise their judgment about the project as a whole, with all the facts in front of them, and have full opportunity to question the responsible ministers with regard to it. That is the basis of our objection to this method of procedure.
It seems to me, sir, that in the circumstances in which we find ourselves, we are asked to use a procedure which, so far as I can recollect, has been used in the past

South Saskatchewan River Project for approval of agreements with foreign countries where no expenditures were involved, though no doubt the Prime Minister will have precedents of a different character. Not having had the time or perhaps the assistance to do research that he has had, some of those precedents may conceivably have some superficial resemblance to what we are embarking upon today; but I should be immensely surprised, sir, if at any time the two houses of parliament have been asked to embark upon a great project of this kind, involving a very large expenditure of money, by the use of this particular device.
I do know that there have been instances in the past when there have been agreements with foreign countries where expenditures of moneys were involved and in those instances, as was the case with the treaty of Versailles itself, legislation was introduced. The treaty was not approved by this particular method. Indeed, my recollection is that this method has generally been used for agreements that did not involve expenditure at all, though I do recall one occasion when a motion of this kind was made to approve a trade agreement. I believe that was not proceeded with, and if my recollection serves me right it was not proceeded with precisely because it was represented that it would be a bypassing of the full rights of parliament to discuss the matter in every possible respect. I think that was in 1947 or 1948, about 10 years ago. Again I have not the precise reference at hand.
As I said, we are faced with a real dilemma here. The Leader of the Opposition indicated -and I think it was one of the first statements he made after he became the leader of our party-that he favoured in principle proceeding with this great national project. As the leader of our party he has indicated the support of our party in principle for the project. As I say we are faced with the choice of voting against this motion and thereby having it represented that we are against the project, or voting for it and being told subsequently, "Well, you approved of that agreement; you have no right to criticize it."
It seems to me that as between those two not very attractive choices we can choose only the second. The only course we can take is reluctantly, because of the method being used, to support this motion. But in saying that I speak for myself, and I am sure I speak for most of the other members of my party, though I have not consulted all of them, when I say that we do not feel that in voting for this resolution we are expressing any approval whatsoever of the details of the agreement. I do not feel that we should


be asked to approve the details of the agreement without going through the proper parliamentary processes; and we reserve the right, when this matter comes before parliament for the appropriation of money in whatever form it may take, to criticize anything in the agreement that in the light of the practical experience of executing it seems to be deserving of criticism.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext: You have pretty well boxed the compass, have you not?

subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as one representing a constituency, namely the constituency of Macleod, which has within its bounds the headwaters of the South Saskatchewan river watershed, the headwaters which will supply the South Saskatchewan dam, I think I might be permitted to say a word or two on behalf of those who are living in that area and also in the various other areas which are served by the South Saskatchewan watershed system.
I think we should all take a look at the riparian rights of the different industries and different sections of the country which are fed by that water system. I am greatly in favour of the South Saskatchewan development. But we must regard it as only one development, on the South Saskatchewan watershed. To the west of it lies the city of Lethbridge. I should like to bring to the attention of the house and of the government the serious problem which exists at the city of Lethbridge with respect to water supply for industrialization. I refer particularly to the month of February. The Oldman river which is a tributary of the South Saskatchewan and joins the river at Lethbridge is almost dry in February. Industrial development of that area is contingent upon the continuity of the flow of water and so the development of dams and other structures in the headwaters of the Oldman river is long overdue. This is related to the waters of the South Saskatchewan dam. In other words-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext: Order. I have not read the agreement, but I doubt if there is anything in it with relation to the damming of the Oldman river.

subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext:
When I talk about the waters of the South Saskatchewan watershed it is just like talking about the relationships of so many balls in a bowl. When you move one ball all the other balls shift to a new position. If you use water out of the river at Lethbridge you are affecting the continuity of flow of water which will run the turbines and provide irrigation at the South Saskatchewan dam. Therefore when I am

talking about the watershed and the South Saskatchewan dam I am, I hope, talking on the subject.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext: I cannot accept that proposition from the hon. member for Macleod, and I hope he will confine himself to the motion under consideration.

subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I shall try to do so. Having covered that point, may I say that so far as the South Saskatchewan river dam is concerned, I have heard many arguments that the production which may flow from the farms will disturb the prices of agricultural products. We all know that in the establishment of an irrigation system there is a time lag of six to eight years before the system is brought into operation. There is also a period of some 25 years before the complete shift in production from dry to irrigated farming takes place. In other words the growth of population, the time lag in development and so on will make the situation such that the incidence of production with regard to the agricultural price structure will not be felt to any extent whatsoever. Therefore from an economic point of view I think that problem can be dismissed.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I wish to compliment the government for undertaking this project, which is the first step in the development of the South Saskatchewan watershed system.

subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a member representing a British Columbia constituency concerned for many years, about the development of its hydro resources, I rise to express my support for the principle of the resolution. However, like some members of the official opposition, we would have preferred the government to bring the matter before the house in the form of legislation which we could discuss in principle, followed by a discussion of the various clauses of the bill. We would have had the opportunity to ask the Prime Minister questions, which we all enjoy doing, and to deal with the various details of this very interesting and worth-while project.
Regardless of the part of Canada from which we come, I am sure we all recognize that the government's decision in this respect is of benefit to the whole of Canada and of particular benefit to the province of Saskatchewan. There is no question but that it will provide greater stability of income, more security and improved standards of living for the people residing in the area that will be served by the dam.
Personally I am very pleased to see such measures introduced, because they provide for the conservation and development of our
South Saskatchewan River Project natural resources. The government has assisted the maritimes with respect to hydro development. Millions have been spent in the development of hydro resources on the St. Lawrence seaway; and while the hydro development was undertaken by the province of Ontario it was the federal government expenditure that made it possible. Now we have this very fortunate development in Saskatchewan. I hope these developments are segments of a national policy that will mean that the government intends to bring a measure before the house in the very near future providing for the development of hydro resources on the Columbia.
I am trying to keep in order, Mr. Speaker. In view of the conversion of the premier of British Columbia to the principle of protecting Canadian rights on the Columbia, and as a result to the development of the water resources of the Columbia under public ownership in co-operation with the federal government, we all hope that agreement in principle with respect to downstream benefits will soon be arrived at between the governments of Canada and the United States and that we shall see the implementation of the policy of development of hydro resources continued by the commencement of the development of the resources of the Columbia.
If I were to go further, Mr. Speaker, 1 think I might be out of order. In any event, we are all very pleased to see that this development is being proceeded with, because of the value it will be to the province of Saskatchewan. Once again I say we hope it represents a policy that will be pursued and which will be continued in British Columbia.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. E. Pascoe (Moose Jaw-Lake Centre):
subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, so much has been said over the last number of years with regard to the South Saskatchewan dam that there is very little new that is left to say. But as the elected representative of the constituency of Moose Jaw-Lake Centre I feel I must express to the government the thanks and appreciation of my constituents for the decision to start construction of this great project. I am happy to endorse the remarks of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, whose constituency adjoins Moose Jaw-Lake Centre.
It was an occasion for celebration when the Prime Minister and the Minister of Agriculture signed the agreement respecting the dam in the presence of the other 15 Progressive Conservative members from the province of Saskatchewan, including the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. To mark the occasion the Saskatchewan members had a picture taken as

South Saskatchewan River Project an historic record of having been part of a government that keeps its promises.
The agreement was signed on July 25. I mention that date to emphasize the speed with which one more promise of the government has been carried out. It was carried out as promptly as possible in spite of provincial politics attempted to be played during the negotiations about the sharing of costs. I am sure that all Canada will commend the government for its quick action to honour a pledge made to the electors. The dam has been too long delayed. In answer to a question I asked on July 2 the Prime Minister stated, as recorded on page 1829 of Hansard:
-climatic conditions in Saskatchewan this year indicate how necessary it was that this dam and irrigation project should have been proceeded with at least six or seven years ago.
This is a statement with which we in Saskatchewan will agree most heartily, especially the livestock farmers who are short of feed this year because of the dry weather during the summer. In his statement on July 2 the Prime Minister also outlined the financial terms of the agreement with the province of Saskatchewan. I do not agree with the charges of the Saskatchewan premier, or the remarks of the hon. member for Assiniboia this morning that the province has been discriminated against as far as the sharing of costs is concerned. I think the terms of the agreement are very generous. They were fully explained by the Prime Minister on page 1829 of Hansard, and were outlined by him again this morning.
I shall not attempt to review those terms here, but I repeat that I think they are most generous and most helpful in regard to the construction of the dam. This dam will assure the cities of Moose Jaw and Regina of an adequate supply of water in Buffalo Pound lake for their future domestic and industrial needs. Letters I have received, and I know the Prime Minister has also received similar letters, indicate that Moose Jaw greatly appreciates this help in solving its long-time water problem. I am sure Regina appreciates this help also.
Some constituents of Moose Jaw-Lake Centre will benefit directly from the irrigation canals, and all the province will benefit indirectly from the agricultural and industrial advancement resulting from the dam. For these reasons in particular, and because of the many other benefits that will result in a wider field, I speak for all in Moose Jaw-Lake Centre and commend the government for making this long-time hope in Saskatchewan a reality.
Today we heard in this house what I consider to be indirect Liberal opposition to the construction of this dam. We were hoping,

we were almost certain, that the Prime Minister's motion would have received quick and unanimous approval. I still hope that this unanimous approval will be given here today, now that the Liberal delaying amendment has been ruled out of order.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext:
I rise to take part in this debate, Mr. Speaker, because of the remarks that have just been made by the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre. He said that what we are now witnessing in this house is indirect opposition to this project on the part of the official opposition. What he had expected to see, and what he had hoped to see, was quick and unanimous approval of this resolution. He had hoped to see quick and unanimous approval of this kind of resolution, unprecedented in our parliamentary history, this kind of resolution which would commit us to approval of an agreement for the expenditure of many millions of dollars.
The hon. member who just spoke said that what he had hoped to see was quick and unanimous agreement, without discussion presumably; because debate on this resolution was commenced today about 12 o'clock, so we have been talking about it for a couple of hours. However, even that is too long for the hon. member who just resumed his seat for us to be dealing with a resolution of this importance which entails the expenditure of many millions of dollars and deals with a project of national significance. If we cannot spend a few hours on a resolution of this kind without being accused of obstruction, then the Prime Minister's talk about parliamentary rights and other rights about which we are going to hear a lot during the rest of this week, does not mean very much.
Then the Prime Minister, in an interjection which may or may not be in Hansard-he will pardon me for mentioning it, but it was quite clear across here-said that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, when he sat down after speaking on behalf of our party, had very successfully boxed the compass.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext: I did not say "successfully".

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext:
Well, that he had boxed the compass; I withdraw the word "successfully". The Prime Minister's intervention at that time seems to me to be quite eloquent evidence of what the Prime Minister may have had in mind in submitting this resolution in this unprecedented form. What the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate did when he spoke for our party, made it quite clear that we were not going to fall into the trap which had been set by the introduction of this resolution in this form. As he pointed out very clearly, and perhaps it could be repeated, if we carry

our objections-and they are sincere objections-to the form of this resolution to the point where we vote against it, now that our amendment has been ruled out of order, then it will be stated by hon. members opposite

indeed it has already been indicated by the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre-* that we are opposed to the project itself. If we vote for the resolution we vote for a resolution in a form which we think does deny the right of parliament to discuss it in the approved form which has been followed in the past in matters of this kind.
The St. Lawrence seaway development, the trans-Canada pipe-line development and other projects of national importance involving the expenditure of many millions of dollars were proceeded with by means of a resolution preparatory to the introduction of a bill. There was discussion of the resolution and the bill. It was possible to examine the agreement, if there was a financial agreement, as a basis for the legislation, also it was possible to examine the minister in detail to find out what was in the agreement and why. We have no opportunity to do that on this particular resolution, which is in the form usually followed in connection with agreements between Canada and foreign states. It is in the form of a resolution which asks us merely to approve an agreement; and if we do approve it, and in so far as we are concerned we are going to vote for this resolution-

subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext: Are you?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext: We are going to vote for it for the reasons I have indicated, because if we vote against it we will be accused of being opposed to the project, and that is exactly the position in which the Prime Minister wished to place us by the introduction of the resolution in this form.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman does not want to ascribe motives. I do not mind the conclusion, but when he says the Prime Minister wished to place him in that position, he knows that that is not right.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext:
I will not ascribe any motive to the Prime Minister; I will withdraw that. I shall describe what will happen as a party. We have already described ourselves as in favour of this project. This was done first of all on February 28 by me, speaking for the party, in Saskatoon, and it has been stated since in the house. We approve of this project as one of national importance. Yet, Mr. Speaker, approving the project as we do, recognizing and appreciating its importance, and with some realization of the expenditure of money involved, we take strong exception to the procedure that is being followed in this
South Saskatchewan River Project resolution, whatever the motives may have been which inspired the government to proceed in this way. We are being asked in this resolution to approve of an agreement, not to approve of a bill which could be discussed in committee and at all its stages. We are not being given an opportunity to question the government in respect of this agreement.
When the Prime Minister rises to close this debate, that will be the last chance we will have to deal with this agreement, certainly in this parliament. If in the future we wish to discuss this matter and the way it is working out, if we take exception to this agreement, if we find some clauses are not as we hoped they would be and that the agreement should be changed, we can and no doubt will be told by the government, "You supported this agreement in the house on Labour day, 1958; what are you complaining about now?"
This is another reason why we object to this kind of procedure. Surely we have the right, now that we the opportunity, to object to this way of proceeding on constitutional grounds. We do not intend in the future to be told that because we have put forward these constitutional objections we are hesitant about the value of this project, or that we attempted to oppose it indirectly, as has already been suggested.
The hon. member for Assiniboia this morning mentioned the position of our party in regard to this matter, and said that he regretted the stand taken by the prime minister of previous years, namely Mr. St. Laurent. I would like to put on record Mr. St. Laurent's last statement on the South Saskatchewan river dam, which was made in answer to a question asked on April 12, 1957, I believe addressed to him by my right hon. friend who is now Prime Minister, and which reads as follows:
My position is that I have not yet been able to reach the conclusion that it is something which, constructed at this time, would return to the national economy more than it would require from the national economy in interest and amortization charges.
Mr. St. Laurent took this position after careful consideration, and he took it with honesty and with sincerity. Believing as he did in it and because that is the kind of man he was, he stated this position frankly to the House of Commons and did not take refuge in any weasel words that could perhaps have gained him some political support and by which he may have indicated that he was in favour of the project at some time in the future but that he would have to look into it and see whether it could be worked out later and all that kind of thing. He got up in the house and explained that having given it the consideration which he felt it

South Saskatchewan River Project should be given, he could not convince himself that at that time it would return to the national economy more than it would require from the national economy.
It is no secret that during those years when this matter was under consideration by the previous government the former minister of agriculture did support the project and did his very best to convince his colleagues that they should also support it. There will be no person in Canada who will more rejoice in the initiation and completion of the project than Mr. Gardiner himself. It is also no secret, because I have mentioned it on more than one occasion, that this party under its present leadership did take a different position in this matter from that taken by the party under its previous leadership. I myself and my colleagues came to the conclusion last February that this is something which should be proceeded with in the national interest. While perhaps on the strict ground of economic returns in the years 1958, 1959 or even 1960 it will not be justified in the light of the money that will have to be spent, there are, nevertheless, considerations other than economic returns. There are intangible and psychological benefits and, adding up all these things, we felt that this was a project which should be supported and so we do support it.
Having said that, I return to our difficulties over the procedure adopted in this matter because we are not being given an opportunity during this session to examine the government in detail in respect of the agreement on which this project is based. It is true that the agreement was tabled many weeks ago-I forget the exact date-by the Minister of Agriculture.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext: August 1.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext:
Perhaps the house does not remember, however, that when the agreement was tabled in this house, without prior notification-and I am not complaining about that-it was done on the last day of the minister's estimates, so we did not have an opportunity even in connection with the Department of Agriculture estimates to examine the minister in respect of this particular agreement at this particular session. If it had been tabled a week before we would have had that opportunity; if the estimates had been held over for a week we would have had that opportunity. But in fact we have not had that opportunity, and are now being asked to support this kind of resolution in order to give a blank cheque to the government in respect of the carrying out of an agreement upon which we have not had a chance to examine the government


in detail. Surely that gives us the right to complain about the procedure adopted in this very important matter-

subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext:
-a procedure which not only violates precedents but also violates parliamentary traditions and parliamentary rights. Therefore, while we support this resolution because we have no alternative but to support it, since we are in favour of this project, we nevertheless reserve our right to bring up this constitutional question again. We also reserve our position in regard to criticisms which we may advance in the future with respect to the detailed working out of this agreement. We have not been given that chance now, but we will certainly take advantage of any opportunity in the future.
I know what the Prime Minister is going to say when he gets up. He is going to say, "You will have ample opportunity to discuss this matter on the estimates next year or the year after that. There will be ample opportunity for the opposition to discuss this agreement; there will be ample opportunity to discuss all these things on the estimates." If that is the case, then what was the purpose of bringing forward this resolution in this form at the present time? What purpose does it serve; what constitutional purpose or what discussion purpose does it serve, when we cannot examine the government in respect of the agreement on which the resolution is based? It is quite true that we may have an opportunity in the future of discussing the agreement on the estimates. If that is the case then perhaps the Prime Minister will explain why, in these closing days of the session, he has brought forward a resolution in this form which does, as I have said and as I now repeat, violate parliamentary traditions; which asks us to support an agreement involving the expenditure of many millions of dollars, and which is in a form as I believe, having regard to all the circumstances, unprecedented in our parliamentary history.

speakeroldname: Hon. Alvin Hamilton (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know you will be relieved when I say I am going to deal with the South Saskatchewan river dam rather than with the constitutional issue which at this time has been dragged in. I shall leave discussion of that issue to others who may speak later.
I would like to place on record at this time some of the efforts made for many years and by many people on behalf of this great project. It was mentioned earlier in the debate today that some Indians on the bank of the South Saskatchewan river had first mentioned

the idea, and that was a good story with which to start a speech; but I would like to place on record an official document submitted to the legislative council of Canada in 1859 by Henry Youle Hind, M. A., professor of chemistry and geology at Trinity College, University of Toronto, who was sent out in the year 1858 to explore the Assiniboine and Saskatchewan river systems on behalf of the government of Canada of the time. I promised myself many years ago that the work of this man of exactly 100 years ago should one day be remembered and now it is acted upon by this government.
I am going to read sections from paragraphs 16, 17 and 18. Firstly, in speaking of the South Saskatchewan river paragraph 16 reads as follows:
A dam, 85 feet high, and 600 to 800 yards long (a few miles lower down the length of the dam would be much less) across the deep narrow valley in which the south branch flows, below where the Qu'Appelle valley joins it, would send its waters down the Qu'Appelle valley, thence down the Assiniboine past Fort Garry, and thus establish a splendid and probably uninterrupted navigation, for steamers of large size, for a distance exceeding 600 miles.
He was thinking 100 years ago of this dam as a means of communication across the whole prairies for 600 miles. Then in paragraph 18 he speaks of the possibility of flooding the towns along the Assiniboine, such as Portage la Prairie, Brandon and Winnipeg, and he speaks of the Assiniboine and the peculiarities of the valley as follows:
Here the river glides in an excavated trench about 16 feet below the prairie, but in times of very high floods it sends water across the prairie, down the broad, shallow valley of Rat Rivulet, into lake Manitoba. Rat Rivulet rises in the Bad Woods, west of Prairie Portage, within two or three miles of the Assiniboine; and the ridge which divides it from the river is an imperceptible rise in the prairie which the eye can scarcely detect.
A shallow cut through the gentle rise separating the Assiniboine from Rat Rivulet would permit all flood waters to flow into lake Manitoba, and protect the settlements on Red river from any danger of being flooded.
And now, 100 years later, a report is being handed to this government concerning lake Manitoba and lake Winnipeg recommending the same cut to save these cities from being flooded. At this time I think it is well to give credit to those who so long ago saw the possibilities of diverting and damming the waters of the Saskatchewan river system.
In more recent times one thinks of such men as John R. MacNicol, a member for one of the Toronto ridings-I believe it was Danforth-who made known to newspaper editors in eastern Canada the possibilities of water control and diversion on the South Saskatchewan. In one year, out of his own pocket, he spent $37,000 on the services of
South Saskatchewan River Project engineers and surveyors who examined this proposition, and it turned out that the figures he supplied agreed almost exactly with the conclusions reached after the expenditure of many millions of dollars under P.F.R.A. in examining the same proposition.
Then, turning to those here today, credit has been given very briefly to the work of the Prime Minister in speaking across Canada and particularly in the west on behalf of the dam. In addition, his speeches here in this house, his questions and his motions, probably did more than anything else to convince the people of western Canada that here was a man who was pledged to this project and who never quibbled or used weasel words about its economic future. For that reason many of us from the west joined forces behind the Prime Minister and recognized in him the person best able to lead those forces across Canada, a man who was thinking in terms of national development rather than in terms of stagnation and allowing things to drift. I think at this time that as one of the younger men in the west who rallied behind the Prime Minister and struggled for the achievement of this project I should like to pay a tribute to him on behalf of all those people who looked to him as their champion.
The house may not even be aware of it today, but when the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar made, I believe, his maiden speech, he was speaking with a record of service toward this project hardly equalled by anyone. He is at present vice president of the Saskatchewan river development association and over the long, difficult years he went about his part of Saskatchewan calling meetings of farmers, municipal boards, boards of trade and so on advocating the building of this dam. When I think of all the hours of driving and the hours of hard work which have been done by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, I wish he was here at this time to hear what I am saying.
Along with others-the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Pascoe), the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Jones), the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. More), the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Nas-serden) for example-many of us have helped in this work and there were others, too, of all political affiliations who did their best to let Canada know that this scheme was in the national interest.
I do not intend to deal at any great length with the benefits the dam will bring, because they have been discussed so many times over so many years by so many people. However, I should like to emphasize just one benefit which I do not think has been fully realized.

South Saskatchewan River Project This dam is not just for the irrigation of farm lands; it is not just for the development of power. It will have many uses.
This new dam will give us in western Canada a chance to bring in industry. With the discovery of natural gas in the last five years we have now, for the first time, an opportunity to bring in the petrochemical industry which requires large amounts of water for cooling purposes. This is a benefit which is just as important as any other benefit which this scheme provides. Speaking solely on this question of industry, the matter of the surplus of power over the needs of pumping is something which has not been appreciated by many who have been great supporters of the project. I think they have failed to recognize the full significance of this development to the three prairie provinces, and I am taking the liberty of reading a quotation from the royal commission report at page 188 where reference is made to this aspect which has been almost forgotten. The report says:

In other words, one of the great benefits of the dam at Coteau creek is that it will not only produce 325 million kilowatts annually for the distribution system of the Saskatchewan Power Corporation in this locality, but that it will increase the potential of five downstream power dams. This is a point which has been forgotten, and I hope the province of Saskatchewan will visualize that it will be one of the great assets produced by this joint operation between the provincial and the federal governments.
I should like to make a passing reference to the benefits to the tourist trade. With this lake a new body of water some 135 miles will come into being. It will give us 475 miles of new shoreline. Sixty-nine per cent of the
[Mr. Hamilton (Qu'Appelle).l
population of Saskatchewan will live within 150 miles of this large body of water, and it will be available to them for recreational use. I should like to remind the house that in the United States where they keep extensive records of visits to national parks, national forests and recreation areas, it has been found that every year more people visit reclamation projects similar to this than visit their national forests or their national parks. This will give to Saskatchewan, one of the dry areas of the world, its first opportunity to have a large lake area right in the heart of the settled portion of the province.
The next subject I should like to mention is one which has been discussed already at some length in this debate, the frank admission on the part of the hon. member for Villeneuve this morning that this dam is now in the national interest. This is a phenomena which those of us from Saskatchewan and the three prairie provinces generally will recognize as a revolution of outstanding importance.
The previous prime minister was praised on many occasions because he was intellectually honest. He was opposed to the dam and he said so. Immediately upon the election of a new leader of the Liberal party there was a change of opinion. In February we heard that the party was in favour. What was not in the national interest a few months before suddenly became in the national interest. I wondered as I listened today how the front benches of the official opposition were going to handle the situation. I wondered, after all the years of stonewalling and delay, what they were going to do and how they could explain their conversion to acceptance of this important scheme. When I heard the amendment moved by the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Dumas) and seconded by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan) I thought, that is their approach; they will let the backbenchers carry the blame for the conversion and the front benchers will keep quiet. But the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) spoiled my analysis of the situation. He felt he had to enter the debate and when he came up with the ingenious proposition of a constitutional principle I saw how he could stand up and claim that he was still fighting a good rearguard action for those opposed to the dam.
I do not know who opposed the former minister of agriculture in the cabinet but since it has been mentioned here by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) that the former minister of agriculture was in favour of the dam I can only assume there must have been some one in the cabinet of the previous administration opposed to it. I could not help but contrast the attitude of the

previous government with the attitude of the present administration. Here we have a government thinking and working only toward having this old political football brought to a happy conclusion. In spite of some provocation and obstruction this government has moved forward and signed an agreement. The agreement was tabled August 1 in this house. And then suddenly, as a smokescreen, we have had this type of diversion on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite. As I look at this thing it leads me to believe this is either an effort to fight a delaying action on the bill-

Mr. Speaker, we are not interested in small-time diversions. We are interested only in the diversion of this water for useful purposes.
I am just going to put it bluntly to those in the front benches of the official opposition. When you speak about a man who is not used to using weasel words, think of the other connotation we can put on that expression.
Since these national benefits are now accepted by the official opposition it is interesting to point out to hon. gentlemen opposite that we are the only ones who have accepted this proposition on the basis of the report of the royal commission. I take it they have now repudiated the royal commission's report and its findings.
There has been some suggestion that the cost would be the same figure they show here. I assume they have repudiated the recommendations of this commission and therefore I can now go on and speak about the other argument that has been put forward in this house and in western Canada dealing with the question of the cost of this project to my province of Saskatchewan. I believe I can do it best by asking hon. members to make a simple comparison.
The federal government over the next eight years will have to put up $75 million cash plus some additional amount of say $11 million or $12 million by way of a loan, making a total of $87 million. On an annual basis this averages out to approximately $11 million per year. The provincial government during this same eight-year period will be putting up $12 million cash for the dam. It will be paying half of the $25 million which is its share in the form of a loan from us which it will
South Saskatchewan River Project have to pay back. The power will cost between $24 million and $35 million. I may tell the house there is no exact figure yet. The province's share of the penstocks will come to about $6 million but its share of the irrigation under a term the provincial government itself has asked for will be only approximately $8 million over the next eight years. And if you add up all these amounts including the full amount of the loan it comes to approximately $73 million or so. Over an eight-year period it will be an average of approximately $9 million. That is what the provincial government of Saskatchewan will be asked to put up each year. It will pay $9 million as opposed to the $11 million paid by the federal government.
Let us put the provincial payment of $9 million into perspective. I presume some of the money will be spent by the Saskatchewan power commission. I refer to the $24 million to $35 million. This year in Saskatchewan the commission is planning to borrow and spend $60 million for expansion of electrical and gas services for the province of Saskatchewan for one year alone. An additional $9 million a year for all irrigation and power expenses combined is a small figure compared with what is spent each year for the usual development and expansion of electrical and gas utilities in that province. This point should be kept in mind.
There has been some discussion about this government being discriminatory against Saskatchewan because last year the federal government made money available to provinces in the maritimes for power development under two bills, one relating to the Beechwood project and the other relating to the Atlantic Provinces Power Development Act. I should like to draw a comparison here. The sum of $30 million was advanced with respect to the Beechwood project over an eight-year period and has to be paid back. The government will also advance periodically as the need arises money for thermal power plants and transmission lines. The money will be loaned on a 30-year and 40-year basis and will have to be paid back.
We are also trying to help the coal industry. We believe the money thus spent will be of great assistance in maintaining this industry at a level of production that will keep the industry going until long range plans are brought into effect. I should like to point out that all the money advanced to the maritime provinces either for the Beechwood project or thermal power has to be paid back and in addition we have asked the maritime provinces to concentrate the advantages of all this financial assistance into the provision of cheaper industrial power.

South Saskatchewan River Project Those are the key things to remember about the maritimes side of the deal.
It is true that in Saskatchewan we are only advancing one-half of the provincial share of the dam on a 20-year basis. That was a concession not given to them in any previous agreement by any government and we have extended this concession. Where in the maritimes deal is there approximately $75 million being given without it being paid back? I believe that is the answer to that point of view.
In concluding I wish to mention that the hon. member for Villeneuve referred to page 90 of the report of the royal commission where it is recommended there should be a single administrative authority over the waters of the entire Canadian west and I believe the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Kindt) was working around to the same suggestion. I should like to point out that this report was given to the government in 1952. I can find nothing in the records to indicate that that particular recommendation or suggestion in the report was ever acted upon. This government came into power just a little over a year ago, and already we have made great steps forward in getting plans ready for the conservation conference to deal with this matter of water resources and their use all across the country. We are moving forward with this type of program.
Over the years many of us have recognized the great necessity of considering our country, not on the basis of narrow provincial boundaries but on the basis of all the provinces working together to help each other. We have had at least two examples to my knowledge in the last little while of provinces working together and getting more power cheaper because they did work together. It is true that this recommendation in the royal commission report is a long range solution to the whole problem of dealing with the resources of western Canada. Eventually, it will have to be looked at as a regional problem and it will take some time to get it into operation; but I think the effective answer is that we are in action on this very fundamental thing.
I have spoken on this resolution with some feeling because I think back now to the many long hours of work and the many long drives that some of us have had trying to make the farmers and the business people of western Canada realize that the only way we can get out of our difficulties in western Canada, where we are so dependent on the ups and downs of prices and of crops, is to do something to conserve this water moving through to the sea without being used. As I look back over the years and think of all those who were with us I realize that to us this

is truly a great agreement, and I hope that it will be remembered for many years.

The resolution before us reads:
That it is expedient that the houses of parliament approve the agreement between the government of Canada and the government of Saskatchewan respecting the South Saskatchewan river project, signed on the 25th day of July, 1958, and that this house do approve the same.
This resolution, if approved, concludes the matter. What is usual in this type of subject matter and this type of question is a resolution reading like this:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to approve the agreement between the government of Canada and the government of Saskatchewan respecting the South Saskatchewan river project, signed on the 25th day of July, 1958.
The latter, and the correct procedure, would give all hon. members an opportunity to question the ministry in committee of the whole house on two occasions, namely at the resolution stage and again at the committee stage of the bill. I wish to ask the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources what is it that he does not want to be questioned about when he takes the extraordinary procedure of introducing this resolution. What is it about this project that he does not want discussed? What information is he not willing to give or is not able to give? Why this extraordinary procedure? I point out to him that in the latter part of his remarks he gave information as to the financial implications flowing from the agreement, but he did that after the house had been debating this measure for some time. I do not think anyone can find anywhere in the record any words spoken by the former prime minister indicating that he was opposed to the project. On numerous occasions he said that he was in favour of it, that is was a desirable thing to do, but he pointed out that we were engaged in the other developments mentioned by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) such as the St. Lawrence seaway, Trans-Canada Air Lines and the pipe line and that this project would have to compete with other projects of that kind. My main purpose in intervening in the debate is to re-echo the hope expressed by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) that this resolution will mark another step forward towards the development of a national policy respecting the development of water resources. In the course of negotiations Ottawa has insisted that Saskatchewan should assume responsibility for operating and maintaining the dam when it is completed. We are, therefore, seeking some assurance that Saskatchewan and its citizens will be safeguarded against financial loss in the unlikely event of a failure in the dam following its construction. [DOT]
What the hon. member for Assiniboia has said today amounts to just the same thing. This statement is absolutely incorrect. The original agreement which we offered to the province of Saskatchewan provided that we would operate and maintain the dam in perpetuity in the same way as we operate and maintain the St. Mary's river dam in Alberta, and the agreement went forward on that basis. There was never any question about that. But the premier of Saskatchewan thought they should take over the operation of the dam. It was their request; they asked to take over the operation. We did not ask them to do it. They asked us and we agreed to it. At the same time, though they wanted to take over the operation they wanted us to be responsible for the maintenance. I pointed out the difficult situation which would result if one government was responsible for maintaining the dam and another for operating it. Difficulties between the two bodies would constantly be arising and it just would not make a reasonable undertaking. Premier Douglas agreed with this point of view, and he agreed to take over both the operation and the maintenance of the dam. Other aspects of the agreement were modified in consequence.
Then, after the whole thing was done and sent to be signed-after we had made a lot of concessions in the light of what had been agreed to-Saskatchewan made a demand that we should assume both the operation and the maintenance of the dam. be completed for six or eight years may not prove to be correct because if prices go down the cost will be less, and if prices rise the cost will be more. I would point out there is an item included which provides for a gradual rise in prices.

As a matter of fact, three of the greatest experts on earth-filled dams in the world have been consulted in connection with this matter. They have been consultants to this project for several years past. I think the estimate is a good estimate. I am not predicting that it is going to cost exactly that amount because no one knows what will happen in the next eight years with regard to prices going up or down.
The next point the hon. member wanted covered was when does the government intend to begin this work and the answer is that it has already begun. Tenders for the first piece of work in connection with the construction of an access road 12 miles in length from a main highway near Loreburn to the damsite were put out immediately after the agreement was signed. I believe tenders closed on August 18 and I expect to be able to announce the awarding of the contract almost immediately.
Tenders have also been put out or are in process of being put out for construction of the campsite. A tender will also be put out for another access road. This does not involve the building of a road but calls for putting a gravel surface on a municipal road which already exists, to give access to the north to highway No. 15 which runs east and west, north of the dam.
Another contract to be let very shortly is for the preparation of the aggregate which will be needed to go into the dam. Another contract will be for the building of a work bridge required for construction purposes. All these will be called for this fall and work will be started on them. Another is the excavation-

The next question was in connection with the function of the construction board. That is set out in detail on page 15 of the agreement. I do not think I had better take the time to go over what the functions of the construction board will be. That board will consist of four members appointed by the federal government and three members appointed by the provincial government. Generally speaking the function of the board will be to exercise a sort of general supervision over this work as it proceeds during the time the dam is under construction, and particularly it is to serve as a body through which any difficulties which may arise between the federal government on one hand and the provincial government on the other hand can be ironed out and decided upon.
The next question related to the time in which the work is to be completed. The estimates in connection with this question vary between six and ten years. These estimates have been made by various people. Most people who are qualified to judge think the dam will be completed in a period ranging between six and eight years. No precise estimate of the time can be given because that will depend to a considerable extent on the amount of flooding which comes down the river each year as the work is in progress. If there is a particularly high level of water it will hold back construction for a considerable length of time each year. As I say, because the speed of construction is going to depend on the weather and also, of course, on the difficulties that may be encountered, no more precise estimate of the time of construction can be given than six to eight years.
The hon. member for Villeneuve also raised a question about whether there would be one large contract for this dam. I believe he expressed the idea that a considerable number of people were of the opinion that that is what should be done. Is that not correct?

We are following exactly the reverse procedure. We think it is very much wiser on a project of this nature to let smaller contracts for two reasons. First of 57071-3-280
South Saskatchewan River Project all it gives many more contractors an opportunity to tender and therefore you get more competition, more bids and lower prices. There will be the various contracts I have mentioned that will be let this fall. There will be six separate contracts and I suppose six different people will get them. In addition to that if you let one large contract for the whole project most of the work would be subcontracted anyway by the large contractor and it is impossible for a contractor to give a firm price on something which is not going to be completed for eight years. The only sort of price they will give is one which has an escalator clause in it. We considered it very much wiser to have small contracts. As I say, it gives a greater opportunity for smaller Canadian contractors if it is let through a series of contracts as the work progresses at a time when contractors are in a position to know definitely the prices for which they are prepared to do the work. Also if you let it in one large contract there is only a limited number of people in this country who would be able to undertake it and if there were only one large contract it would be more likely that the contract would be secured by someone in another country. For all those reasons we considered it much wiser to let it in a series of smaller contracts.
I believe I have covered most of the points that were raised. I have not gone into the many values of this project.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
