speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. C-57, for approving certain expenditures authorized for the public service, and the application of certain amounts in the accounts, of the financial year ended the 31st March, 1958.

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: Has the minister any additional comments to make?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I doubt if there is anything I might usefully add to what I endeavoured to say on the resolution stage preceding the introduction of the present measure. The resolution was before the committee of the whole on August 19 and August 20, when I had an opportunity to make certain comments by way of explanation of the report on supply and the effect of the present bill. The debate is reported at page 3808 of Hansard for August 19 and at page 3822 and following pages of August 20. By this report on supply we have, I believe, fulfilled the undertaking given to this house on the opening of the present session and have fully accounted for the three governor general's warrants included in the approving provisions of the bill now before the house.
I pointed out at page 3809 of Hansard for August 19 that the house is being asked to approve of supply which was released, whether in the form of appropriations made

Finance-Special Warrants by parliament or by governor general's warrants. The house is not being asked to approve actual expenditure as such. The actual expenditure will be duly reported and, after audit by the Auditor General and included in the public accounts for the fiscal year 1957-58.
I have drawn attention to eleven items which are contained in the fourth column of the report on supply and which aggregated $110,042,595, and fully explained the purpose of those items, which are of a transfer or legislative character.

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: I fully realize that in what we hope will be the last week of the sittings of this particular session of parliament, when a member rises there is always a little consternation in some sections of the house and there is perhaps among some members the feeling that a debate of this kind is being unduly prolonged. It is true that in the bill we are considering here we are dealing with the bringing forth for debate, after a denial of the right, of certain governor general's warrants which were passed in the fiscal year 1957-58. Speaking as I do on one side of what might be called a no man's land ditch consisting of a big group of surplus Conservative members on my left, I realize their feelings but I must point out to them that they too often give unqualified, uncritical and, I think, all too generous support to the proposals of the administration. So it is the duty of the opposition, however small, to draw certain matters to the attention of the house. I wish to indicate to some of these new members just why debate is sometimes prolonged, and why I feel obliged to say something on this matter at the present time. Many hon. members are in the house today who were not in the house during the previous parliament-

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: And many hon. members are not here today who were in the previous parliament.

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance had certain comments to make on this bill about some economies he had introduced as a result of a few months of office. I just want to say to the new members that sometimes debate would not be so prolonged if some of the ministers introducing bills would stick to the facts and not engage in overmuch boasting or what I call peacocking about. Very quickly after assuming office the Minister of Finance gave a press interview on June 26, 1957, indicating there would be vast reductions in expenditure and economies as a result of the elimination of extravagances which he expected to find. And probably, in deference to that very widely publicized statement which was made in June,
[Mr. Fleming (Eglinton).l
the minister felt obliged in December, when he was making a financial statement, to make certain assertions to the house which I suggest do not hold water. Then the other day when he introduced a resolution preceding this bill he did the same thing and I suggest to hon. members that that is why there is an obligation on those of us who do not accept such assertions in an unqualified way to make some remarks at this time.
On December 6, 1957, the Minister of Finance in his financial statement which was sometimes called the baby budget but which was in fact a discussion of the first item of the estimates of the finance department of that year, felt obliged to stick out his chest and assert that the new administration was providing economies to the extent of some $170 million. We know that $100 million of that had reference to two provisions which had been cautiously put into the budget for the year by his predecessor with respect to sums which will eventually have to be paid. If these are eliminated from the accounts of last year there is nobody who studies the accounts of this country who does not know that both those items of $50 million each will eventually be a charge on the taxpayers -it was simply a matter of whether the expenditure would be deferred until another year or whether it would be taken in the accounts of the fiscal year which the hon. minister's predecessor proposed. One was an allowance against the reserve for assets and the other was a $50 million appropriation for a deficiency which actuaries tell us is in the superannuation account and must be made up sometime.
The minister indicated, of course, that beyond this there were some other things which he took great pride in claiming as economies and as savings due to the elimination of waste as a result of the change of adminis-tation. Again, not being too anxious to get legislation of this kind through in the present session when we had our first reference to governor general's warrants and appropriations for supply, in the new parliament on May 13 the Minister of Finance said he had succeeded in reducing the amount of the estimates which had been drawn up-he was referring to last year, the year we are discussing now-and tabled by the previous government that by efforts-I emphasize efforts-in the various departments of government the sum of $73.6 million had been eliminated.
It is bold, unjustified and boastful assertions of that kind which demand a reply. I have checked, and I find it is not unusual to have in almost every year what are known as lapses. The public accounts of 1956-57 which were tabled this session indicate that

the lapsing-the items that have been put earlier into the book of estimates but which at the end of the year were not fully spent- amounted to $86 million or 3 per cent. In the previous year 1955-56 lapsing amounted to $136 million or 4 per cent. I may say that none of these items have any reference to such items as appear in the document we will be studying more closely in a few minutes entitled "Loans investment and working capital advances". In the year before that, 1954-55 lapsing amounted to $359 million or 11 per cent, and in 1953-54 lapsing amounted to $309 million or 9J per cent. So I do not want new members to take seriously some of these assertions in introducing a measure of this kind such as I think the Minister of Finance is a little too prone to make. He is introducing a financial statement and I think we would make better progress if it was divorced from provocative political assertions which I think after examination do not bear much examination.
Similarly, when we discuss warrants and general business administration under appropriation bills we find it necessary to return to another assertion which, I say, was completely, political and unjustified, namely, the assertion by the Prime Minister in the course of the election campaign when he took a lot of figures together which totalled, I think, $1,185 millions. He referred to these as being public works items which would help to deal with the employment situation. Two hundred and eighty million dollars of this amount, he said, would be spent in the last quarter of the last fiscal year ending on March 31, 1957 and the impression was given to the public that this was something unique, something wonderful and different by reason of the right hon. gentleman's administration. We are dealing this afternoon with the appropriations which were recommended under the governor general's warrant including the last quarter of the last fiscal year, because parliament was not then sitting and instead of there being any increase in the category of public works and work-creating measures there were actually, in several categories, reductions under governor general's warrants as compared with the proposals which were introduced by the previous administration.
I might say in passing that this business of lapsing is a fairly normal one and when one looks at the time table of the preparation of government business and estimates one can readily understand how that would come about. The estimates are for the fiscal year commencing in April and they are normally examined by the treasury board and finally approved before Christmas in order that the blue book of estimates for the new year
Finance-Special Warrants commencing April 1 which we all receive shortly after parliament opens can be printed. One therefore recognizes that when the Minister of Finance in December 1957 made reference to certain economies against the background of the book of estimates prepared by his predecessor he was referring to estimates which had been prepared a year earlier. Consequently one can understand that there would be certain changes of plans and that within three months of the conclusion of the fiscal year every department of government could probably foresee, either some delay in getting plans or materials ready or the postponement and in some cases the abandonment of projects which it had seemed desirable to put in hand 12 months earlier. That is actually what we are dealing with now, but when I challenged the minister with it on August 20 when we were dealing with the resolution which proceeded the introduction of this bill, I obtained no reply.
One can look at the column in the bill which refers to things that the minister has always asserted were economies and savings. I asked him very definitely how much of this actually represented the cancellation of programs and the elimination of plans and how much was really in fact a simple deferment of the things we would be called upon to revote and doubtless in the current fiscal year. Perhaps the minister will recall some of the illustrations I gave him. Since that debate on August 20 we have had several references in this house to some of the larger items of this $73 million so called savings item.
We had a statement the other day from the ministry pointing out that they take pride in the fact that there was a step-up in sales of wheat and flour as a result of our contributions under the Colombo plan. 1 pointed out that the saving of ten million on the appropriation of last year would doubtless be picked up in the current year. We examined the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) with respect to maritime freight rates on Saturday and where there was a claim for an economy there we found it was a statutory item. I asked the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Brooks) whether or not the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) had gone to him and asked him to scrimp a little bit with respect to disability pensions and veterans allowances. I could tell from the smile on the face of the Minister of Veterans Affairs and knowing him as I do that no economy was attempted in that sphere as claimed.
But nonetheless items of this kind are all part and parcel of this $73 million that has been presented to the people as savings and economies as a result of a change of administration. I say that interestingly enough they

Finance-Special Warrants compare with the lapsing and normal procedure that concludes the final accounting of every fiscal year of which I have given an illustration for four or five years.
The biggest item of the $73-odd million, of course, refers to the Department of National Defence. Here there is a claim of a saving of some $32 million. Again I have looked to the relationship between the maximum amount voted by parliament in previous years and the amount that might be expended by that department when the final accounts for the year are completed. In 1956-57 which is the last year which the Auditor General has reported upon to this house I found there was a lapsing in National Defence Department of $15,990,000. The previous year 195556 there was an underspending, shall I call it, of some $25 million and in the year before 1954-55 the underspending was no less than $242 million.
On December 5 in the last session I tried, I thought fairly valiantly, as did Mr. Henderson the former hon. member for Kingston, to get some breakdown in detail with respect to the savings that were represented in this item of $32 million. We were not very successful in our attempt. In a broad way we received some information from the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes) which appears on page 1903 of Hansard. I will not repeat that in too much detail but it refers to such an economy as the transfer of the ship Labrador from his department to the Department of Transport. It also refers to the cancellation of further production with respect to the CF-100 aircraft. I have no doubt that probably any administration examining an item that had been decided upon one year earlier with respect to something as volatile as decisions in the aircraft business would probably have reached that decision.
There was also some boasting about savings in travelling expenses of the troops. We have had a very extensive study of the defence department expenditures in the estimates committee and we found that there is to be a savings this year with respect to transportation but when we probed as to the reason we found that this is not one of the years when there will be a rotation of the troops in Europe which is an extremely expensive proposition and that it has now been decided to do this every three years and any very large saving is accounted for by this. It is such an attractive suggestion to say to the public that one has reduced travelling expenses!
This is just an illustration of the undesirability in presenting what is essentially a business statement of introducing it with preliminaries that are definitely of a political

character and must receive challenge in an assembly such as this. It is in the public interest that that be done.
As the minister has said, we have discussed the general question of governor general's warrants previously. We have done so on May 13 and 14. We discussed the Financial Administration Act on July 29 and I made reference to the history of bringing to this parliament an examination of these warrants at that time as I did on August 19 as reported at page 3766 of Hansard and on August 20 as reported at page 3822 of Hansard. I wish to point out, however, without repeating myself that there certainly is a Doctor Jekyll and Mr. Hyde complex on the part of the Minister of Finance. When we regard his appreciation of the rights of parliament with respect to supply when he was sitting in opposition and the attempt that was made on February 1 by the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) to say that the law would be satisfied irrespective of historic practice if the Minister of Finance simply announced his governor general's warrants to the house without debate.
The minister, of course, said we had had debate. We had it because we were debating on a point of order and not because the government decided to give us that historic privilege. I also wish to remind the minister that in the debate on May 14 we had a little argument as to just how much of the estimates of the 1957-58 fiscal year had received attention in the committee of supply in the last parliament and I think he said that more than one half had been approved. It is true that we had interim supply bills with respect to the ten-twelfths and in some instances with respect to the eleven-twelfths but I find that only five departments received discussion that could in any way be considered fairly full and six departments received partial consideration before dissolution of the parliament of last year. We also noted that the departments which were of particular public interest because of the economic crisis did not come before parliament at all. I refer to the Department of Labour, the Department of Public Works and the Department of Transport.
I must say we are grateful that there was a change of mind and heart with respect to the decision about giving us no opportunity in the committee of supply to consider governor general's warrants in some detail, a tradition that has existed since time immemorial. I congratulate the Minister of Finance for the form in which the information has been prepared. It was available at the time of the resolution and also appears as an appendix to the bill. I have no doubt that in committee we will be able to proceed item

by item if there is a desire, and this is a very convenient form of discussion.
Before concluding I wish to say that I have noticed all throughout this session another extremely undesirable practice setting in and some reference was made to it the other day by the Leader of the Opposition and myself; that is that we are asked in committee of supply to give consideration to the activities of the departments without having available the latest official report on the activities of the department. I believe it was an oversight, but it happens that the second biggest spending department of the government actually broke the law. There is a statute which says that within a certain period of time they must provide the House of Commons with a report on the activities of the department. I refer to the Department of National Health and Welfare which is making expenditures, statutory and items in the estimates, that exceed $1,200 million. We found to our great surprise and inconvenience, and to our great loss in the value of our work in committee, that when we were asked to examine the estimates of the Department of National Defence very closely in committee-and we spent a lot of time on them-we were greatly handicapped to find that for the first time for years we had neither a white paper which previous ministers had always prepared for the use of parliament in advance of the discussion of the ministers' estimates nor alternatively, and usually both, the annual report.
I admit immediately that to our great surprise when we examined the statute with respect to the Department of National Defence we found that there was no statutory obligation to submit an annual report to parliament. I think that that should be drawn to the attention of the administration. It is the biggest spending department; it is spending $1,700 million. I do feel that annually this house and the public at large should not be deprived of a statement, either a white paper or an annual report, or both. I can certainly say that when one who is not naturally abreast of the developments of this sphere is asked to give hours and hours of attention in close study in committees, which are meeting several times a week for two hours at a stretch, one is exceedingly handicapped when he finds that the last available information to him is something that happened in 1956. Surely that is a sphere upon which we must be up to date if we are to bring effective thought and criticism to bear upon it.
I want to point out that there may be other instances, but I think that this is a tendency that must be deplored. I do not think my hon. friend can suggest very many precedents for this in the past unless the 57071-3-281
Finance-Special Warrants calendar was responsible for it. It was not something that was too coincidental or, shall I say, deliberate? Maybe this sessions events are not deliberate. But perhaps there was no department this session that we were more concerned about examining with the best possible background than the Department of Labour.
I found that within a few days after the minister was released with respect to his estimates we were able to get in our mail boxes the last annual report of that department. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) indicated to the house the other day in an inquiry of the minister, which may be found at page 4162 of Hansard that the very important report of the advisory council with respect to unemployment insurance was available to the cabinet on July 31. In the meantime, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) had his estimates before the committee of supply. A couple of days after he was released and his estimates passed we got this report in our mail boxes. I say there is something radically wrong in what seems to be the trend in this respect, and I must advance the strongest possible protest. Our opposition may not be too large but because of the fact the government, as never before in the history of this country, has so many supporters one would think it would be all the more anxious to make sure that the best possible information at the earliest possible date is made available to the opposition. I can recall the many eloquent speeches of my hon. friend in the past, advancing the importance of the role of the opposition in our parliamentary life and government.
There are some items in the schedule that I should like to ask the minister about. Perhaps in particular we shall hear from him at the committee stage something about the old age pension situation because that transfer or an appropriation of $103 million is the largest item in the total of $114 million that comes under the category of increases and not decreases.

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in this group approve the principle of this bill which is to seek parliamentary approval for certain expenditures that were incurred without previous approval owing to the dissolution of parliament. I cannot help but bring to the attention of the house the fact that this group fought very hard last session in support of the very procedure that the government is adopting in the introduction of this bill, which at the time seemed unpopular to certain members on the government side who expressed that feeling during that debate which took the better part of an afternoon and an evening. However, we are very glad that the government has listened
4438	HOUSE OF
Finance-Special Warrants to our arguments, and apparently has gone over those arguments in between the sessions and by the introduction of this bill has come to the conclusion that we were right. There is no question about it, Mr. Speaker, in our opinion the government was on very shaky constitutional ground last session with respect to the failure to produce certain estimates on immigration, I think it was, when they were under discussion in the house, seeking expenditures which had been occasioned as a result of governor general's warrants.
We may have some questions to ask at the committee stage but at this time I wish to conclude by congratulating the government on its recognition of the validity of our argument last session and on its repentance in between sessions and also on its position, as a result of our appeal, in finally restoring to parliament its rights in respect of the introduction of this bill.

No, Mr. Speaker. I should like to say just a word or two but I am not going to make a speech. The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) said that his group approved the principle of this bill. I do not think that we can approve the principle of the bill. As the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) has said, we think the government has done the right thing in bringing those warrants before parliament. We think that is the proper thing to do. Of course, that is what a distinguished member of the C.C.F. party and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) both asked in the last parliament should be done. But it seems to me that if we voted for this bill we would be not only approving having warrants brought here for our consideration but we would also be giving our approval to the government in spending a great sum of money in February and March by governor general's warrants and we most emphatically do not approve of that.
Our position is that the government had no excuse whatever for that dissolution, not the slightest excuse, except the desire for power.

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: That is over with.

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: Oh, yes. Those hon. gentlemen who do not seem to understand very much what parliament is about say that that is over with, that is done. That is certainly right-

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: One-man party.

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext:
That is exactly the point I was trying to make. This avid desire for 

power, seizing the moment regardless of parliamentary institutions, is what has made it necessary for the government to bring this bill now. The government, having got an overwhelming vote of confidence from the previous house, should have stayed here and carried on with the nation's business and had the money voted by parliament for that purpose. We feel that if we voted for this bill we would be supporting the course taken by the government which we think was not justified except, of course, by the success at the polls. While we do not contest that, we do contest as a matter of principle the way it was arrived at.
I am just going to say one word about the possible parallel. It is true that on January 25, 1940-the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) will correct me if I am wrong- parliament met in the morning and was dissolved in the evening. It is true that the government of that day did have to use governor general's warrants for the new fiscal year up until May 16, 17 or 18, 1940, when parliament did provide further money.
But I would point out that there are three very important respects in which the two situations differ. In the first place, that was already the fifth year of that parliament. There had to be an election some time during that year. We were in the midst of a war and it was very important, if at all possible, to have the election at a time when there would be the least possible disturbance of the nation and the least possible disturbance of the time of ministers; in other words, at a time before the real fighting began. By the dissolution at that date that was accomplished.
The second difference, of course, is that the government of that day had been challenged, it is true not in the house but outside it, by the premier and the leader of the opposition of the largest province and there was an urgent need to discover whether that government or some other government should be entrusted with the supreme duty of carrying on the war.
The third, and in a technical sense the most important respect in which the two situations differ, is that supply had already been voted months before right up until March 31 so that there was no question of using warrants while the election was on. There was no question of using warrants before the election which, if my memory serves me correctly, was on March 26 and, of course, supply had been provided until March 31. Whatever the outcome of that election it would have been a government with a fresh mandate from the people which

would have used warrants for the short interim period between the election and the opening of parliament.
My attention has been drawn by the member for Kenora-Rainy River in this connection to something said by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) when he was sitting on this side of the house. In a debate on interim supply on April 28, 1949, he said, as found at page 2898 of Hansard:
-the government had moved closer to the election and they had carefully investigated all aspects of their supply problem, because when the Prime Minister arrived in Ottawa last Saturday on his return from his western tour he was met by the press and this question of supply came up. If you please, sir, the Prime Minister informed the press that financial supply could be authorized by governor general's warrants instead of by votes in the House of Commons. That is the statement of the Prime Minister. Why are we here? Sir, we are apparently just going through some motions here, because the government has already decided that whether it gets a vote of interim supply or not, it is going to spend whatever money it wishes to spend between now and the date on which the new parliament will assemble. Did you ever see, sir, any more bare-faced renunciation of responsibility-
This is the Minister of Finance speaking about Mr. St. Laurent.
-to parliament, any clearer evidence of the fact that this government has treated parliament, is treating it today as it has treated it hitherto, with studied contempt? This was a carefully calculated statement by the Prime Minister and we may be sure that he made it after due consideration.
What happened in 1949? In 1949 we- not "we"; I was not here-the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) and other hon. members, including the Minister of Finance-

He conducted himself in the proper constitutional fashion, as the Minister of Finance said he should have done. He did not show the contempt for parliament which, according to the Minister of Finance, was shown to the previous parliament on the first of February.
For these reasons and many others I could add we cannot support second reading of the bill.

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext:
This, I think, is the key to the whole reason for departure from making it open to the committee of supply to debate governor general's warrants in subsequent sessions of parliament. We all know that we had an election in June of 1957 and the administration that replaced the old one on June 10 of that year made a great deal of political capital about what had been done for Hungarian refugees. I am quite confident that the reason there was a desire to not have subsequently a debate about governor general's warrants was the fact that while they had criticized not only these allowances but their immigration itself even though the recent minister of citizenship and immigration, the present Minister of Justice, told my friend the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate that he had not gone far enough with Hungarian immigration. I believe this is the item that explains the whole reason why the new government departed from the traditional system of giving an opportunity in subsequent books of estimates and in subsequent meetings of the committee of supply to debate any item that was involved in the governor general's warrants.
One will see here extra funds were required by the new administration for this purpose. They apparently decided it was desirable and in the public interest and should be continued and they went to the governor general and got the warrant to make that possible. But in so far as bringing it up in the subsequent session of parliament for debate was concerned, they tried to avoid it and I well realize it was because of what they had to say in the 1957 election campaign.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the amount in question was provided by special warrant and the purpose of it is described as follows. Perhaps I should read the warrant:
Pursuant to order in council P.C. 1957-1134 of 19th August, 1957, the Minister of Finance and Receiver General is hereby authorized to pay, out of any unappropriated moneys forming part of the consolidated revenue fund, the sum of $2,428,000 (in addition to the sums already granted under vote 71 by the Appropriation Act, No. 3, 1957, and the Appropriation Act, No. 4, 1957) to provide, subject to the approval of treasury board, for expenditures in respect of transoceanic and inland transportation and other assistance for immigrants and settlers, including care en route and while awaiting employment.
That warrant was duly gazetted. It appeared in the Canada Gazette of August

Finance-Special Warrants 31, 1957, and a copy of it was tabled in this to February 1 that this amount was going house at the beginning of the next session, to be cut. I could be wrong about that. I in October, 1957.	just wonder whether that is so.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: Shall Indian affairs branch carry? Shall national gallery of Canada carry?

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: I notice that the amount in the estimates was $130,000; the amount authorized was $108,334. I also notice that in the estimates we passed the other day this amount was cut down to $100,000. Is it the policy of the present administration to reduce the annual grants to the national gallery?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: It would not be proper for me to make any comment on the 1958-59 estimate. So far as the 1957-58 item now before the committee is concerned, I simply point out that when the warrant was issued in early February we did not go one cent beyond existing commitments. That is the reason for the reduction of $21,666.

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: What does the minister mean by "existing commitments"?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: Existing commitments as at the date of the issuance of the warrant. My hon. friend will recall that the special warrant in question was issued on February 7.

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: I presume the minister means that this amount represented the difference between 10 months and 12 months, or does it go up to February 7?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: It means that in drawing the warrant on February 7, so far as purchases for the gallery are concerned, there was none provided for, for the remainder of the fiscal year to March 31. In other words, the appropriations at that point stopped with the commitments as they stood at that date.

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: I do not quite understand. I may be exceedingly stupid about this, but I do not understand what the minister means by "commitments" because he surely realizes that whatever is appropriated is paid into the purchase account. There is no question of any commitment of any kind. The government decides to recommend how much parliament should have to pay into the purchase account and the gallery may not have spent that that year at all. It had been the practice for a number of years to appropriate $130,000 for this purpose and I would have thought, this being in the estimates and fractions of it having been voted on two or three occasions, it was an implication on the part of the government that they intended to appropriate the full amount for the fiscal year. I do not think we were given any indication up

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: In submitting to His Excellency in early February the warrant for his approval the cabinet considered that in this respect it should not go beyond the commitments that then existed. If parliament had been sitting and had chosen to come forward and appropriate the full $130,000 that would have been one thing; but in drawing the warrant for submission to His Excellency for his approval cabinet felt that it should not go beyond the commitment existing at that date.

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: I do not understand what the minister means by "commitment", commitment to whom?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: These are actual commitments for purchases of paintings at the date the warrant was drawn.

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: Is the minister sure of that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext:
Can he produce any
evidence of that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: That is the information I received.

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: I must say I would like more than just that statement to satisfy me. However, if I cannot get it, I cannot get it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: Shall civil service commission carry? Shall defence production department, A, carry?

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext:
Perhaps my remarks
would be related to all the items of so-called savings under defence production. I note they total not quite a million dollars? These, of course, are all part and parcel of the claim that $73 million of savings had been created. These are items of capital assistance for construction and for defence construction, I think largely housing, for service people in the forces. Are these real cancellations of the program or are they deferments?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: Is my hon. friend referring specifically to item 89?

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: Items 89, 91 and 92.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext:
Perhaps we had better take them one at a time. Item 89 provides for capital assistance. There was a deceleration of the production of the CF-105, a cancellation of certain equipment for that plane and a lower than anticipated cost for the FN rifle project. That figure is $499,265.
Then, on item 90, which is the provision for payment of grants to municipalities in lieu of taxes on crown-owned defence plants,

Finance-Special Warrants the difference of $26,000 is accounted for by the fact that under the terms of lease with Canadian Pratt and Whitney Limited that company will pay the taxes on the plant at Longueuil. Under item 91, under crown companies, there was a slow-down in the over-all defence construction, accounting for the reduction of $211,021.
Item 93, under Canadian Arsenals Limited, the difference was owing to the same cause.

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the minister very kindly drew to my attention when we were on the resolution stage the five items before us that are dollar items.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: Yes, there are five.

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: I do not think I have a quarrel with respect to the others but I am curious about the fact that there is no language to explain the reason for $1 for administration and operation of Canadian Arsenals Limited. Is that simply for the purpose of debate?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: Under Canadian Arsenals Limited, the item is provided to permit the operation of the plant. It is a matter of purchases and sales, and this is the item under which discussion can be had.

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: There are some crown companies that have not even got an item of $1 in our estimates. Is that so?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: Yes, there are some crown companies, it is true, to which there is no direct reference in the items of the estimates. My hon. friend can recall some, for instance, that report to departments such as defences production or trade and commerce and which are normally discussed for that reason under the first item of those departments.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext:
Shall external affairs
carry?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: There is a reduction in item 97 of $356,000, for construction, maintenance and rental of buildings abroad. Is this merely a deferment of the construction program or is it an abandonment of some part of the program which had been planned?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: The proposal for construction of a chancellery in Canberra and the residence in Brussels was not proceeded with last year. The department's limited technical resources were fully occupied with other projects.

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: None the less, is it going ahead this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: I think I will have to leave my hon. friend to raise that point on the 1958-1959 estimates.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: I think the 1958-59 estimate has shown that they were proceeding with them this year.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: Shall general carry? Shall North Atlantic treaty organization carry? Shall international civil aviation organization carry? Shall international joint commission carry? Shall terminable services carry?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: There is an item here, 797, which shows a reduction of $10 million for the purchase of wheat and flour to be given to India, Pakistan and Ceylon to relieve food shortages. Would the minister be good enough to explain to the committee what this reduction means because it is our understanding that these amounts have been increased this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: They have been increased this year. So far as this item is concerned, arrangements for shipment could not be completed before the end of the fiscal year.

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: So that particular saving of $10 million also out of the $73 million did not require all the hard work that the minister said he was going to put into savings and economies compared with the previous estimates?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: This item is not one related to economy. This is an item that was provided for last year and for the reason I have given, because arrangements for shipment could not be completed before the end of the fiscal year, the money was not required. But my hon. friend is well aware of the program in the 1958-59 estimates.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: I take it that the result of this would be that in the wheat statistics of the previous year this amount of $10 million will not show. There will be a reduction to that extent and that $10 million will be shown in the current statistics of wheat and flour shipments under the new vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext:
Yes. Obviously nothing is going to be shown as applied to
1957-58 that was not provided in that year. The figure for 1958-59 will make the provision intended for the present fiscal year.

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext:
It is not quite as simple as that. This is the item in the estimates of the Minister of Trade and Commerce where he tried to show the sharply increased wheat exports this year in terms of bushels of wheat exported. That is something I think we are all very glad to see but in his effort to do so it was not clearly demonstrated that

there was a comparison made with the previous year whereas there were merely deferred shipments that had been provided for in the previous year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: My hon. friend realizes that this is only part of the item. There was provision made for $15 million of which wheat to the extent of $5 million was shipped.

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: I quite realize that, Mr. Chairman, but I want to point out that this is the very difficulty we were trying to have clarified on the estimates of the Minister of Trade and Commerce.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: I was not present when they were being discussed.

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: There is one question I am sure the minister can answer. When did this $15 million first appear in the estimates? I suppose the minister should tell me that I ought to look that up myself but I have not done it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: It appeared in the supplementary estimates which were tabled last autumn. I will have to obtain the exact date for my hon. friend, but I think it was in the further supplementary estimates, No. 2.

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: In other words, it was anticipated in the autumn that $15 million would be required and in fact only $5 million was required before the end of the fiscal year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: The hope was that arrangements could be made for shipment of the full amount covered by the sum proposed to be appropriated. Part of it was shipped, but not all.

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext:
But this is one of the
items of the $73.6 million referred to on page 18 of Hansard of this session when the minister was dealing with accounts for the previous year, when he said savings had been effected.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: I would not be able to answer that question without looking it up. I know it is part of the items I referred to on August 19 at the resolution stage.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: There is an item here, 795, for the provision of technical assistance to the West Indies and to Ghana and a saving of $135,000 is shown. I take it that is merely a deferment of that expenditure to the current year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext:
That program was initiated in February, 1958, which left less than two months before the close of the fiscal year. Within that short period of time it was possible to post only a small number of technical experts prior to March 31. The hon.
Finance-Special Warrants gentleman is aware of the plans for technical assistance to the West Indies in the fiscal year 1958-59.

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: Would that explanation not mean that the provision of the item of $150,000 in the previous estimates when they were presented would be quite misleading because it was obvious that the money would not be spent in that fiscal year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: It was not misleading at all. Parliament was asked to provide the money, and every attempt was made to employ and post technical experts. However, in the time available it was not possible to post more than a small number of technical experts prior to March 31. It was not for lack of effort, I can assure the committee.

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: What item is this in last year's estimates?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: It is item 795.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: Shall terminable services carry? Shall finance, general administration carry? Shall administration of various acts and costs of special functions carry? Shall public debt charges carry? Shall payments to municipalities carry? Shall contingencies and miscellaneous carry?

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: I am not as familiar as I should be with the Financial Administration Act. This, of course, is an item to delete from the accounts certain debts due to and claims of Her Majesty, each of which is in excess of $1,000, amounting in the aggregate to $627,411.15. Will these appear specifically in the public accounts?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: My hon. friend is referring to item 689?

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: My hon. friend is aware of the provision that has been made in the recent amendments to the Financial Administration Act in connection with the deletion from the public accounts of debts due to Her Majesty. Item 690 simply contains a form of authorization, which is the form employed hitherto prior to the amendment to the Financial Administration Act, under which treasury board derives authority to delete from the accounts debts due and claims of Her Majesty, each of which is in excess of $1,000, amounting in the aggregate to $627,000 odd.

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: Do they appear in the public accounts?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: Yes, they do.

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext:
Because I notice that 689 appears to be in the form of legislation.

Finance-Special Warrants I do not know whether or not this is something we have done before but in 689 it does say specifically that these items shall be reported in the public accounts whereas under 690 the same clear provision is not present.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: They are referring to two different things.

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: Oh, yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: Originally when 689 was introduced it was intended to authorize the making of regulations by treasury board providing for the deletion from the accounts of certain debts due Her Majesty. It was our feeling that sort of item should not be a method of legislation. That was the reason for introducing specific and continuing statutory authority.

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: It is superseded by the recent amendment to the Financial Administration Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: Recently, yes.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: Shall contingencies and miscellaneous carry? Shall special carry? Shall general items of payroll costs including superannuation payments carry? Shall university grants carry? Shall miscellaneous grants carry? Shall fisheries, general services, carry? Shall field services carry? Shall international commissions carry? Shall special carry?

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: On special, Mr. Chairman, item 159 is to provide for the operation and maintenance of the Newfoundland bait service. I notice there was a reduction of $100,000. Could the minister tell us what occasioned that reduction?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman, it was not found possible to proceed as quickly as had been expected with the construction of bait facilities at Bonavista, Newfoundland.

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext:
I thought that was it, and
I wanted to say that I still think they are not being proceeded with nearly as rapidly as they should be. As the minister is well aware, there is a very serious shortage of bait in Newfoundland. I do hope he will urge the Minister of Fisheries to do his utmost to see that this delay is not continued any longer than it absolutely has to be.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext:
Special carried. Shall
Fisheries Research Board carry? Shall governor general's and lieutenant governor's carry? Shall insurance carry? The next is Department of Justice. Shall A-Department carry? Shall penitentiaries carry?

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext:
This item 184 is one of
the larger items and there has been a saving claimed of $1 million. Is this a deferment also?
[Mr. Benidickson.l

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: This reduction was made in committee of supply itself on January 10, 1958 at the request of the Minister of Justice.

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: Was it simply because he recognized that construction would not proceed within the fiscal year and would probably go into the accounts of the succeeding year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: Shall labour carry? Shall special services carry? Shall vocational training co-ordination carry?

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: On this item there seems to be a very large saving of $4.5 million. Could the minister explain that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: This item 197, and the sum of $2 million had been reserved in case Quebec signed an agreement. The balance of the reduction was possible because provinces were not claiming the full amounts available in the first year of the new vocational and technical training agreement No. 2.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: Shall government employees' compensation carry? Shall unemployment insurance carry? Shall legislation, the Senate, carry? Shall the House of Commons carry? Shall the library of parliament carry?

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: I wonder what this saving is? Could the minister tell us?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: There was difficulty in recruiting cataloguing staff and that resulted in a salary saving, and there was a lesser amount spent for the purchase of books, microfilming and book repair than was originally estimated.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: Shall pensions and other benefits carry? Mines and Technical Surveys, shall administration services carry? Shall surveys and mapping branch carry? Shall geological survey of Canada carry? Shall mines branch carry? Shall geographical branch carry? Shall dominion observatories carry? Shall general carry? Shall dominion coal board carry? National Defence, shall defence services carry? Shall general services carry?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: On national defence services, there was a very large saving of $32 million. I wonder if the minister would make a statement, and particularly inform us how much of this is due to deferment of construction?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext:
The figure of $32 million is a net figure. The reduction is the result of decreases, at least in the national defence estimates, on portions other than that applicable to defence research board, which is

offset in part by an increase in the provision made for the defence research board. I can give the committee a breakdown, if that is desired.
The decreases are as follows: Departmental administration, $380,000; inspection services, $1,604,267; navy, $6,270,206; army, $20,752,000; air, $6,614,142; defence expenditures by other departments, transport $750,000; mutual aid, $10,716,385, for a total of $47,087,000. There was an offsetting increase in the provision for the defence research board of $15,000,087, resulting in a net reduction of $32 million.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: Could the minister give the committee any indication of the proportion of this saving of $32 million that appears in the current estimates. In other words, how much of this is deferment of expenditure?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: So far as the relationship of the 1958-59 estimates is concerned, that was fully discussed before the estimates committee. It is there as a matter of record. This subject was gone into on a return made to a question put in that committee by the hon. member for Levis.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: Shall pensions and other benefits carry? Shall national film board carry?

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: In view of the sentiments about the film board that used to be expressed by the Minister of Finance when he was on this side of the house, was he not able to find any economies in this service?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: Is my hon. friend referring to any particular item?

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: No, to the over-all picture.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: National health and welfare, departmental administration, shall that carry? Shall health services carry? Shall general health branch carry? Shall grants to health organizations carry? Shall special carry? Shall welfare branch carry?

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext: Was not something provided in connection with this particular item by the previous minister of finance in the way of a definite transfer item?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext:
For the old age
security fund?

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext:
On the old age pensions item you have in the estimates, on the extreme left, $103 million. I take it that when the governor general's warrant was drawn up it was decided to include nothing in respect of this fund. I have every reason to understand why that might be the case. I take it that the original estimate is to be exceeded by almost a million dollars, nine hundred and some odd thousand. What is the present position of the fund? I have a Canadian Press
Finance-Special Warrants dispatch from Harold Morrison which has been widely quoted throughout the country, and I am sure before preparing his article he saw the officials of the department. The article was prepared after the commencement of the new fiscal year. He said it was expected that the total disbursement from the fund this year would be about $555 million, which would be a rise of $118 million over last year, and it was felt that the special taxes that are allocated to the fund would amount to $330 million which would leave a deficit of $225 million. The minister and I had some discussion on that phase at the time of the budget debate and he had some calculations. Then, I think he thought the deficit would be $190 million; I am not sure of that, but I think it was $190 million. It is two months or more since we have had a discussion on this matter. Would the minister make any comment as to whether or not he has a new forecast as to the probable deficit in the fund if new regulations are not provided?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would not care to attempt any new forecast with respect to the present fiscal year, 1958-59, so far as the deficit of the fund for the year 1957-58 is concerned, I think my hon. friend is under a misapprehension in saying that some provision was made in that behalf by my predecessor. I cannot let this pass without saying a brief word about item 723 relating to remuneration for members of the privy council. I think I should like to express once again my feeling that this was a most inappropriate and, I suggest, unconstitutional thing for the governor in council to have done.
It does seem to me that however far they might go in appropriating money for other persons it is carrying the power conferred upon the governor in council under the Financial Administration Act pretty far when it is extended to the point of handing out additional sums of money to members of the cabinet who are themselves responsible to parliament for recommending all appropriations. It does seem to me that this is a function which should have been left exclusively to parliament. I had thought the other day when we had a discussion on the Prime Minister's estimates that the right hon. gentleman was going to get an opinion from the law officers of the crown about this whole subject, and I still hope he is going to do that. I think this is a practice which ought never to occur again, and having said that I do not intend to say anything more about it.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman has not added anything to what he said on a previous occasion on this subject, but so far as approval by parliament is concerned I should like to bring to the attention of the committee the fact that this item was before the previous parliament during the 1957-58 session and that parliament appropriated a portion of this amount in several of the interim supply bills. subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext:
Now if the minister had shown a little more forbearance I should have said nothing more on this subject, but I cannot let that pass. The other day when I spoke on this matter I read two extracts from the minister's statement made on his first interim supply bill last October. He made no mention whatsoever of this item; it was never mentioned as far as I can discover in any of the statements the minister made. It is true it was in the estimates, but the minister said what we were doing there was not in any sense final. It does seem to me that because we in the opposition con-venienced the government by giving them interim supply, that the government should come forward now and say that because we gave them interim supply and because we overlooked something which was not drawn to our attention this indicated there was parliamentary approval, because there was

Finance-Special Warrants not parliamentary approval in any except the most technical sense. And we were considerably abused, if I remember correctly the minister's speech at that time-his manners have somewhat improved since then, I might add-for holding up interim supply as long as we did. I admit it was perfectly legal to make those payments up to January 31 on the basis of the interim supply which was voted, but I think it was a very improper thing and an unconstitutional thing for the government to have done it in the hole and corner in which they did, without the Minister of Finance or the Prime Minister coming here and telling us what was being done. I think it was a wholly inexcusable thing to appropriate further moneys under the Financial Administration Act by governor general's warrant for this purpose.

I must say that is a conclusion with which I would find it difficult to agree. The few cases where the government did see fit not to use warrants were those cases where habitually over a long period of years parliament had appropriated a special sum to go into these funds. The Prime Minister told us when the federal district commission estimates were before us that this practice was followed with respect to the national capital fund but he also indicated that in that case the difference was being made up -and indeed more than made up-in a supplementary appropriation in the current fiscal year.
I drew attention a few moments ago to the item in respect of the national gallery which was reduced in the manner the minister has just described and now we have this one for the national library similarly reduced but in neither of these cases is there any suggestion that the amount should be appropriated this year in any supplementary estimates of which I have heard. It seems to me that these grants which for use and wont have been made for a number of years were precisely of a kind that no one would have taken any reasonable exception to but it is these exceptional and extraordinary items that we find it hard to understand, not items of a conventional character such as this. The extraordinary scruples of the minister in this particular regard do not appeal very much to me.

as was provided for in the 1957-58 estimates
Finance-Special Warrants the Department of Public Works will have some projects that naturally are not proceeded with or not proceeded with to the extent originally contemplated and there will be others which are. Now the extent to which the amounts originally estimated were not fully appropriated in the end is attributable in cases to the sort of situation that I have indicated. It certainly was not due to any slowing down of the program of construction. The situation was fully discussed in parliament in 1957. The rule that was followed was that where any construction project involved the creation of work there was to be no slowdown of the construction program in that regard at all because our concern was for the provision of employment as well as for the provision of needed public facilities.

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would point out to the minister that his answer does not really deal with the point raised. It will be recalled that on February 18, 1958 the Prime Minister announced expected expenditures by government departments and agencies on public works projects totalling $280 million during the first quarter of 1958 and that was put forward across the country as a vastly increased works program that was to assist in meeting the problem of unemployment. While it was not admitted by him that a serious unemployment problem existed apparently he recognized that a need for a program of this kind did exist. As against the statement we all recall was made by the Prime Minister on that occasion we have the facts coming out through these figures showing there was not an increase at all in the first quarter of 1958 but that there was in fact the usual decrease that comes because of the impossibility of estimating precisely what the amount of works will be and the short-falls that are inevitable in any system where you estimate to a definite period and do not carry on the construction for reasons that are easily understandable up to the full amount.
The Prime Minister's statement that was followed up and repeated across this country was in fact of a nature that created an impression in the public mind which was quite contrary to the facts as revealed today by the figures we are now examining and put forward by the minister in his report on supply for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1958.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, that statement cannot be allowed to pass without reply. The fact is we are dealing here with the estimates of the Department of Public Works. The construction program to which the Prime Minister made reference

Finance-Special Warrants on the occasion to which my hon. friend has alluded related to the total construction program of the government embracing all departments.

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think this is an interesting point because it did obtain widespread publicity in February after a certain use was made of certain figures given by the Prime Minister that involved public works expenditures. speechtext: My hon. friend is overlooking the fact that items were added in the supplementary estimates that the new government introduced.

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext:
Oh, there were some supplementary estimates but I think all hon. members well know that supplementary estimates are not to be regarded in any way in the same manner as original estimates for the year round planning of administration. I have before me the estimates for 1958-59 and I agree they are not particularly relevant in discussing 1957-58, except that in each year it is customary in preparing the book of estimates to provide a summary of standard objects of expenditure and special categories. Under buildings and works, including land, column 13 of the new table, an over-all figure is given for the construction and for acquisition of buildings and works, including land, of all departments including public works. I can repeat my point when we come to some of the departments that are to follow. Actually, here is a lapsing of $3 million in public works. On December 6, the minister said that nothing would be allowed to lapse if it could possibly proceed, because of unemployment conditions. Here in public works there is a lapsing of $3 million. I accept his explanation that this is $3 million out of a very large appropriation, but the appropriation was basically provided by the previous

administration. In the main estimates, under column 13, for 1957-58, which we are now discussing, the total for all departments was $374,442,000. The main estimates of the new administration prepared for 1958-59, with unemployment continuing and the administration being very impressed by it as a result of the election activity we all had throughout the country in recent months, provides an increase of only $6 million.
The next comparable item would be purchases of equipment by the government. I refer to construction or acquisition of equipment in column 16 of this summary of standard objects of expenditures and special categories. In the main estimates under this category the previous administration for 1957-58 provided for an expenditure of almost $549 million. The proposals for the current year in the main estimates are almost $548 million, just about the same thing, and conditions at the time of preparing this estimate were entirely different. If as we proceed we keep this debate in mind we will find in the transport department a substantially larger lapse in expenditures on airports and construction of that kind which would have been very worthwhile last winter because of the unemployment situation. We will find under loans and advances even more considerable sums but as long as the administration continues to assert that in the matter of providing public works in tough times it is doing something different from which the previous administration planned to do in December, 1956, when they were fighting inflation I think the time of the committee is well spent in pointing that out.

There are others but they do all throw the spotlight of truth on those exaggerated statements of last February and March about this $280 million crash program of public works for unemployment.
